name: Napoleonic Wars
summary: France under Napoleon fought most of Europe for twelve years and briefly dominated the continent.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). The Napoleonic Wars were a series of conflicts fought between 1803 and 1815 by [Napoleon's](item:napoleon-bonaparte) France and a shifting set of coalitions led by Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia. France won almost every campaign on land for a decade and at its height controlled or dominated most of continental Europe. It was worn down by the war in Spain, by the destruction of the Grande Armée in Russia and by the coalition of 1813 to 1815.

The wars grew out of the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) and the revolutionary wars that preceded them, and resumed after the short-lived Peace of Amiens broke down in May 1803. France's advantage on land rested on large conscript armies, a corps system that could march and fight separately, and a commander willing to take risks for a decisive battle. Britain's advantage was money and command of the sea.

Roughly three to six million people died, soldiers and civilians together. The wars carried the Napoleonic Code, the metric system, conscription and the administrative state across Europe, dissolved the Holy Roman Empire, and contributed to national movements in Germany, Italy and Spain. The Congress of Vienna settlement of 1814–15 restored monarchies but also built a balance of power that kept the great states from a general European war until [1914](event:ww1). Spain's collapse under French occupation also loosened its grip on the Americas, where the [independence wars](event:latam-independence) began in 1810.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars).

steps.name: The rupture of Amiens
steps.page:
The Peace of Amiens, signed in 1802, was the only interval of general peace between France and Britain in twenty-two years, and it lasted fourteen months. Britain refused to evacuate Malta as agreed, France continued to expand its influence in Italy, Switzerland and the Low Countries, and Britain declared war on 18 May 1803.

Napoleon massed an army of invasion at Boulogne and gathered the barges to carry it, which required command of the Channel for long enough to cross.

steps.name: Jena and Auerstedt
steps.page:
Prussia mobilised against France in 1806 and was destroyed in a fortnight. Two battles fought on the same day, 14 October, at Jena and at Auerstedt, broke the Prussian army; Berlin was occupied a fortnight later.

Napoleon then fought the Russians to a standstill in Poland and East Prussia through the winter and beat them at Friedland in June 1807. The treaties of Tilsit that followed left France dominant from the Rhine to the Niemen and brought Russia into the Continental System, the blockade of British trade.

steps.name: The Peninsular War
steps.page:
French troops occupied Spain in 1808 and Napoleon put his brother Joseph on its throne. The rising in Madrid on 2 May and the surrender of a French corps at Bailén in July showed that a Spanish population in arms could not be dealt with as an army could.

Six years of siege, battle and guerrilla warfare followed, with a British army under Wellesley (later the Duke of Wellington) holding Portugal and advancing from it. Napoleon called it his Spanish ulcer; it consumed several hundred thousand French troops.

steps.name: Leipzig
steps.page:
With the Grande Armée destroyed in Russia, Prussia and then Austria changed sides. Napoleon raised a new army of conscripts and won at Lützen and Bautzen, but could not force a peace.

Half a million men fought at Leipzig over four days in October 1813, the largest battle in Europe before 1914. The French were beaten and driven back across the Rhine, and the Confederation of the Rhine collapsed with them.

steps.name: The first abdication
steps.page:
The coalition invaded France from the east while Wellington crossed the Pyrenees from Spain. Napoleon manoeuvred skilfully with a much smaller army through the winter of 1814, but Paris surrendered on 31 March and his marshals refused to march on it.

He abdicated on 6 April 1814 and was given the island of Elba and the title of emperor of it. The Bourbons were restored, and the powers met at Vienna to settle the map of Europe.

steps.name: The peace of 1815
steps.page:
The Congress of Vienna closed its Final Act nine days before Waterloo. It restored the Bourbons, enlarged the Netherlands and Prussia as barriers against France, confirmed the end of the Holy Roman Empire, and set up a balance in which no single power could dominate the continent.

The second Treaty of Paris of 20 November 1815 imposed an indemnity and an army of occupation on France but left its 1790 borders intact. Napoleon was sent to St Helena. The settlement held the great powers back from a general European war until [1914](item:ww1).

name: Battle of Trafalgar
summary: Nelson destroyed the combined French and Spanish fleets off Cadiz, ending any prospect of invading Britain.
body:
Part of [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars). The Battle of Trafalgar was fought on 21 October 1805 off Cape Trafalgar, on the Atlantic coast of Spain south of Cadiz. A British fleet of 27 ships of the line under Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson attacked a combined French and Spanish fleet of 33 under Pierre-Charles Villeneuve. About 22 of the allied ships were captured or destroyed; the British lost none.

Nelson attacked in two columns driven perpendicularly through the enemy line rather than forming the conventional parallel line of battle, accepting fire on his leading ships in order to break the allied formation into pieces that could be beaten separately. He was shot by a musket ball from the French *Redoutable* during the action and died a few hours later, after the outcome was clear.

Napoleon had already abandoned his plan to invade England two months earlier and marched the army waiting at Boulogne into Germany. Trafalgar did not therefore save Britain from an invasion that was still coming, but it destroyed the naval means of attempting one and confirmed a command of the sea that Britain held for the rest of the [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars) and long after. That command sustained the blockade of the French coast and the army Britain kept supplied in Spain.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Trafalgar).

name: Battle of Austerlitz
summary: Napoleon defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army in Moravia on 2 December 1805.
body:
Part of [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars). The Battle of Austerlitz was fought on 2 December 1805 in Moravia, near the town then called Austerlitz and now Slavkov u Brna. Napoleon's Grande Armée defeated a larger Russian and Austrian army under Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, which is why it is often called the Battle of the Three Emperors. It is usually treated as Napoleon's most complete victory.

Napoleon deliberately gave up the Pratzen Heights in the centre of the field and left his right flank looking weak, inviting the allies to march across his front to turn it. When they did, he drove Soult's corps up onto the vacated heights and cut their army in two. Allied losses were about 27,000 killed, wounded or captured, against roughly 9,000 French.

Austria left the war within weeks. The Treaty of Pressburg stripped it of Venetia and its remaining territory in southern Germany, and Napoleon reorganised the German states into the Confederation of the Rhine; the Holy Roman Empire, by then a thousand years old in name, was dissolved in August 1806. Austerlitz also ended the Third Coalition, leaving Britain fighting on alone at sea after [Trafalgar](event:trafalgar).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Austerlitz).

name: Charles Darwin
summary: English naturalist who established that species descend with modification from common ancestors, and proposed natural selection as the mechanism.
body:
Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was an English naturalist who showed that living species are descended with modification from common ancestors, and who proposed [natural selection](item:natural-selection) as the process that shapes them. [*On the Origin of Species*](item:origin-species), published in 1859, set out the evidence and the argument together. It is the foundation of modern biology.

Darwin abandoned medicine at Edinburgh and read for the clergy at Cambridge before sailing as naturalist on HMS *Beagle* in 1831. The five-year voyage took him along the coasts of South America and to the Galápagos, and the fossils, geology and island species he collected there occupied him for the rest of his life.

He worked out the principle of natural selection by 1838 but published nothing for twenty years, spending them instead on barnacles, orchids and correspondence. In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay reaching the same conclusion; their work was read jointly to the Linnean Society, and the *Origin* followed the next year.

Later books extended the argument to human ancestry, to sexual selection and to the expression of emotion. Darwin lived quietly at Down House in Kent, in poor health, and is buried in Westminster Abbey. Descent with modification is now the organising principle of biology, and its union with genetics after the [structure of DNA](item:dna-structure) was established has left the core of his argument intact.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin).

name: Abraham Lincoln
summary: Sixteenth president of the United States, who led the Union through the Civil War and made the abolition of slavery its object.
body:
Abraham Lincoln (1809–1865) was the sixteenth president of the United States. He held the Union together through the [Civil War](item:us-civil-war), made the destruction of slavery one of its objects, and was assassinated five days after the Confederate surrender. He is generally ranked among the country's most consequential presidents.

Lincoln was born in a Kentucky log cabin, had perhaps a year of formal schooling, and taught himself law in Illinois. A Whig legislator and one-term congressman, he returned to politics over the extension of slavery into the territories, lost a Senate race to Stephen Douglas in 1858 after a celebrated series of debates, and was elected president in 1860 on the new Republican ticket.

Seven states seceded before he took office and war began within six weeks. He held the border states, blockaded the South, and cycled through commanders until he found Grant. The [Emancipation Proclamation](item:emancipation) of 1863 turned the war for the Union into a war against slavery and opened the army to black soldiers; his address at [Gettysburg](item:gettysburg) that November restated the war as a test of whether government by consent could survive.

Re-elected in 1864, he pressed the Thirteenth Amendment through Congress and argued for a lenient peace. Five days after Lee's surrender he was [shot at Ford's Theatre](item:lincoln-assassination), the first American president to be assassinated.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln).

name: Latin American wars of independence
summary: Spain and Portugal lost almost all of their American empires within a generation.
body:
Between about 1810 and 1826 almost all of Spain's American empire, and Portugal's, became independent. A dozen new states emerged from Mexico to Chile, most of them republics, in a series of wars fought largely by creole elites against colonial administrations and their local supporters.

The opening was made in Europe. Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 deposed the king, and colonial cities responded by forming juntas that claimed to govern in his name; when the monarchy was restored, most refused to hand the power back. Simón Bolívar campaigned north from Venezuela through Colombia and Ecuador; José de San Martín crossed the Andes from Argentina into Chile and went on to Peru. The decisive land battles were fought at Boyacá in 1819, Carabobo in 1821 and Ayacucho in 1824. Brazil separated from Portugal in 1822 with almost no fighting, and kept a monarchy until 1889.

The new states inherited colonial economies, deep inequality between creoles, mestizos, indigenous peoples and the enslaved, and borders drawn from administrative districts that no one had expected to defend. Bolívar's hope of a single federation failed, slavery lasted for decades more in several countries, and the period of independence wars was followed in most of the region by a long instability of civil wars and strongmen.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_American_wars_of_independence).

name: French invasion of Russia
summary: An army of some 600,000 marched to Moscow; fewer than a tenth came back.
body:
Part of [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars). In June 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia with the largest army yet assembled in Europe, between 450,000 and 600,000 men of a dozen nationalities. Six months later a small remnant of it recrossed the frontier. The campaign destroyed the Grande Armée and began the collapse of French dominance in Europe.

Napoleon's aim was to force Tsar Alexander I back into the Continental System, the blockade of British trade that Russia had stopped enforcing. The Russian armies refused the decisive battle he needed and withdrew eastwards, burning supplies as they went. They finally stood at Borodino on 7 September, the deadliest single day of the Napoleonic Wars, and then withdrew again. The French entered Moscow a week later and found it largely deserted; fire destroyed most of the city, and no offer of peace came.

The retreat began on 19 October, too late in the season. Cold, hunger, typhus and constant harrying by Cossacks and partisans did far more damage than battle; the crossing of the Berezina in late November cost tens of thousands more. Fewer than a tenth of those who had crossed the Niemen came back with the main body. Prussia and Austria changed sides the following year, and by 1814 the coalition was in Paris.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_invasion_of_Russia).

name: Battle of Waterloo
summary: Wellington held the ridge until the Prussians arrived; Napoleon abdicated four days later and died in exile on St Helena.
body:
Part of [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars). The Battle of Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815 a few kilometres south of Brussels, in what is now Belgium. An Anglo-allied army under the Duke of Wellington and a Prussian army under Gebhard von Blücher defeated Napoleon in a single day's fighting. It ended his return to power and the [Napoleonic Wars](event:napoleonic-wars) with them.

Napoleon had escaped from Elba in March and recovered France without a shot, but faced coalition armies assembling on every frontier. He moved first, into Belgium, to beat the British and Prussian forces before they could join. He mauled the Prussians at Ligny on 16 June but failed to destroy them, and they marched to Wellington's support rather than away.

Wellington held a ridge at Mont-Saint-Jean through a day of French infantry and cavalry attacks, with the farms of Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte anchoring his line. The Prussians arrived on the French right in the afternoon and in growing strength; the final attack of the Imperial Guard was repulsed and the French army broke. Casualties on all sides ran to about 55,000.

Napoleon abdicated four days later and was exiled to St Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Waterloo).

name: Eruption of Tambora
summary: The largest eruption in recorded history threw enough sulphate into the stratosphere to cool the whole planet.
body:
Mount Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa in what is now Indonesia, erupted in April 1815 in the largest volcanic eruption in recorded history. It ejected on the order of a hundred cubic kilometres of rock and ash and removed about 1,400 metres from the height of the mountain. The sulphur it put into the stratosphere cooled the whole planet for several years.

The climactic phase began on 10 April and was heard more than 2,000 kilometres away. Pyroclastic flows destroyed the settlements on the peninsula, ash fell deep enough to collapse roofs across the region, and tsunamis struck neighbouring islands. Perhaps 10,000 people were killed outright; many tens of thousands more died on Sumbawa and Lombok in the famine and disease that followed the loss of the crop.

A veil of sulphate aerosol spread through the stratosphere and reflected sunlight for years. Average temperatures in the northern hemisphere fell by roughly half a degree Celsius, enough to shorten growing seasons, and 1816 became [the year without a summer](event:year-without-summer), with failed harvests and famine in Europe, North America and China.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1815_eruption_of_Mount_Tambora).

name: Ada Lovelace
summary: English mathematician whose notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine describe a machine that could operate on symbols rather than only on numbers.
body:
Ada Lovelace (1815–1852) was an English mathematician who wrote the notes accompanying the first published description of Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. They contain a method for computing Bernoulli numbers on the machine, commonly described as the first algorithm written for a computer, and the observation that such a machine could operate on symbols of any kind rather than only on numbers.

Augusta Ada Byron was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, who left England when she was a month old, and of Anne Isabella Milbanke, who had her tutored in mathematics in the hope of steadying an inherited temperament. She met Babbage at seventeen and became a correspondent on his calculating engines.

In 1843 she translated an Italian account of the proposed engine and appended notes three times the length of the original. Beyond the Bernoulli program, they argue that a machine manipulating symbols by rule could compose music or work on anything reducible to symbols, and, in a passage later answered by [Turing](item:alan-turing), that the machine can originate nothing, only do what it is ordered to do.

Neither the engine nor the notes had much practical effect: Babbage never built the machine, and the ideas were rediscovered rather than inherited when electronic computing began a century later. She died of cancer at thirty-six.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_Lovelace).

name: The Year Without a Summer
summary: Snow fell in New England in June and harvests failed across Europe and Asia, causing the worst famine of the century.
body:
Part of [Eruption of Tambora](event:tambora). 1816 is known as the year without a summer. Temperatures across the northern hemisphere fell far enough to wreck the growing season, and harvests failed in New England, across much of Europe and in parts of Asia. It produced the worst famine of the nineteenth century in the West.

The cause was the [eruption of Tambora](event:tambora) the previous April, whose sulphate aerosols spread through the stratosphere and reflected sunlight; a run of weak solar activity and earlier eruptions had already cooled the decade. Snow fell in New England in June and killing frosts came in every summer month, driving a wave of migration from Vermont and New Hampshire towards Ohio and the west. Ireland had eight weeks of rain, and a typhus epidemic followed. Grain prices in Europe doubled or worse, and there were food riots in Britain, France and Switzerland. In Yunnan, repeated failure of the rice crop caused a famine remembered in local verse.

Kept indoors by the weather during a summer at Lake Geneva, Mary Shelley began *Frankenstein* and John Polidori wrote *The Vampyre*. The year is the standard historical example of what a large eruption does to the food supply, and one of the first for which the meteorological consequences were reconstructed in detail.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer).

name: First passenger railway
summary: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first intercity line worked entirely by steam locomotives.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened on 15 September 1830. It was the first intercity railway worked entirely by steam locomotives, carrying passengers and freight to a timetable on a double track, and it is the usual starting point for the railway age.

The line was built to move raw cotton and finished cloth between the port and the mills more cheaply than the canals could. The directors settled the question of motive power with the Rainhill Trials in October 1829, which Stephenson's *Rocket* won; the choice of locomotives over stationary engines and cable haulage decided the shape of railways everywhere. The opening day also produced the first widely reported railway fatality, when the MP William Huskisson was struck by *Rocket*.

Passenger traffic turned out to be far larger than anyone had planned for, and the model was copied at speed. Within thirty years networks covered Britain, much of Europe and the eastern United States. Railways collapsed travel times, created national markets for perishable goods, moved coal and iron in quantities that fed the rest of the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution), and forced the adoption of a single standard time in place of local solar time so that a timetable could mean the same thing at both ends of a line.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_and_Manchester_Railway).

name: Opium Wars
summary: Britain forced China to keep importing opium, taking Hong Kong and a series of unequal treaties.
body:
Part of the [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty) era. The Opium Wars were two wars fought in China in the middle of the nineteenth century: Britain against the Qing from 1839 to 1842, and Britain and France against the Qing from 1856 to 1860. Both ended in Chinese defeat and in treaties that opened the country to foreign trade and residence on foreign terms.

The trade at issue was opium. Britain bought tea, silk and porcelain in quantity and had little the Chinese market wanted in return, which drained silver eastwards; from the late eighteenth century the East India Company balanced its accounts by growing opium in Bengal and selling it to smugglers at Canton, against Chinese law. By the 1830s the flow of silver had reversed and addiction was a public problem, and the Qing court decided to stop the trade at its point of entry.

The wars that followed were short and one-sided. Steam gunboats, rifled artillery and a professional navy were met by coastal forts and an army with much older equipment. The settlements (Nanking, Tianjin and Peking) ceded Hong Kong, opened treaty ports, fixed tariffs by treaty, granted foreigners immunity from Chinese law, admitted missionaries to the interior and legalised the opium trade, and they were followed by comparable demands from France, the United States and Russia.

They are the beginning of what Chinese historiography calls the century of humiliation. They cost the Qing revenue and authority at the same time as the [Taiping Rebellion](event:taiping) in the south.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium_Wars).

steps.name: Lin Zexu destroys the opium
steps.page:
The Daoguang emperor sent Lin Zexu to Canton as special commissioner with orders to end the opium trade. He arrested Chinese dealers, blockaded the foreign factories and demanded the surrender of the stock held there.

The British superintendent of trade handed over 20,000 chests in the name of his government, and Lin had them destroyed in trenches on the beach at Humen over three weeks in June 1839. The Chinese government considered the matter closed; the British government treated the seizure as a debt owed by the Crown and a reason for war.

steps.name: The First Opium War
steps.page:
A British expeditionary force arrived in 1840, bypassed Canton and attacked up the coast. The iron steamer *Nemesis* and ships of the line destroyed war junks and shore batteries with almost no loss, and landing parties took Chusan, Ningbo, Shanghai and finally Zhenjiang, which cut the Grand Canal and the capital's grain supply.

The Qing sued for peace with a British squadron anchored off Nanjing in August 1842.

steps.name: The Treaty of Nanking
steps.page:
The treaty signed aboard HMS *Cornwallis* on 29 August 1842 ceded Hong Kong island in perpetuity, opened five ports to trade and residence (Canton, Amoy, Foochow, Ningpo and Shanghai), abolished the Canton monopoly system, and imposed an indemnity of 21 million silver dollars.

Supplementary agreements added a fixed tariff, extraterritorial jurisdiction over British subjects and most-favoured-nation treatment, which passed every future concession automatically to every other treaty power. Opium was not mentioned. It is the first of the unequal treaties.

steps.name: The Second Opium War
steps.page:
Britain sought a wider opening than Nanking had given and used the boarding of the *Arrow*, a Chinese-owned ship registered in Hong Kong, as the occasion. France joined over the killing of a missionary; the United States and Russia followed the campaign and took the same terms.

Canton was taken in 1857 and the Taku forts at the mouth of the Peiho in 1858, and the treaties of Tianjin were signed. When the Qing refused to ratify them the allies fought their way to Peking, which they entered in October 1860, while the [Taiping Rebellion](item:taiping) was still running in the south.

steps.name: The Summer Palace and the Convention of Peking
steps.page:
After envoys sent under a flag of truce were imprisoned and several of them killed, Lord Elgin ordered the Old Summer Palace (the Yuanmingyuan, a complex of palaces and gardens north-west of Peking) looted and burned. It took two days and 3,500 troops.

The Convention of Peking, signed on 24 October 1860, ratified the Tianjin treaties, opened Tianjin, ceded Kowloon, doubled the indemnity, legalised the opium trade and the emigration of Chinese labour, and admitted missionaries to the interior. The ruins of the Summer Palace have been left unrestored.

name: Electric telegraph
summary: Samuel Morse opened the first practical long-distance telegraph line, from Washington to Baltimore, in May 1844.
body:
The electric telegraph separated the movement of a message from the movement of a messenger. Samuel Morse opened the first practical long-distance line in the United States between Washington and Baltimore on 24 May 1844; comparable systems were already working in Britain, where Cooke and Wheatstone had put a line beside the Great Western Railway in 1839.

The apparatus was simple: a battery, a wire, a key that broke the circuit, and a sounder or a marker at the far end. What made Morse's version spread was the code, short and long pulses assigned to letters by frequency of use, which allowed an ordinary operator to work quickly with cheap equipment. Lines followed railway tracks, which needed the telegraph anyway to run trains safely on single track.

Within twenty years the network reached across North America and Europe, and in 1866 a [cable across the Atlantic](event:transatlantic-telegraph) finally held, cutting the time for a message from London to New York from ten days to minutes. News agencies, commodity and stock prices, weather warnings, diplomacy and military command were all reorganised around near-instant reporting. The [telephone](event:telephone) followed in 1876 and [wireless telegraphy](event:wireless-telegraphy) in the 1890s.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_telegraph).

name: First public demonstration of ether anesthesia
summary: William Morton demonstrated that ether vapour could render a patient painless during surgery at Massachusetts General Hospital.
body:
On 16 October 1846, at the Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, the dentist William Morton gave ether vapour to a patient while the surgeon John Collins Warren removed a tumour from his neck. The patient felt no pain. The demonstration is the usual starting point of surgical anaesthesia, and the room is still called the Ether Dome.

Surgery before the 1840s was done on conscious patients, held down, and had to be fast; the range of operations that could be attempted was limited by how much a person could endure. Ether and nitrous oxide had been known for decades and used at parties before anyone applied them seriously. News of the Boston demonstration reached Britain within weeks, and James Simpson in Edinburgh introduced chloroform the following year, which became the preferred agent in Europe until its dangers to the heart and liver became clear.

Anaesthesia made it possible to operate slowly and deliberately, and so to operate inside the abdomen and the chest at all. On its own it raised the number of operations without making them survivable; that took [germ theory](event:germ-theory) and antisepsis, which arrived twenty years later. Together the two turned surgery from a last resort into a routine part of medicine.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_general_anesthesia).

name: Revolutions of 1848
summary: Liberal and nationalist uprisings broke out in some fifty European states within months; nearly all were suppressed within two years.
body:
In 1848 revolutions broke out across Europe within a few months of each other, in France, the German and Italian states, the Habsburg monarchy and beyond, some fifty countries and territories in all. They demanded constitutions, parliaments, press freedom, the end of remaining feudal obligations, and in central Europe national unification or independence. Almost all had been defeated by the end of 1849.

The background was a bad harvest and a potato blight in 1846–47, a financial crisis, and a generation of educated men shut out of politics by the restored monarchies of 1815. The rising in Palermo came first, in January; the abdication of Louis Philippe in Paris in February set off the rest. Assemblies met in Frankfurt, Vienna, Berlin and Rome; the Frankfurt Parliament drafted a constitution for a united Germany and offered the crown to the king of Prussia, who refused it.

The revolutions failed largely because their coalitions split (liberals against radicals, national movements against each other) and because the armies stayed loyal. Some gains survived: serfdom was abolished in the Habsburg lands, Prussia kept a constitution, and France became a republic, though it elected Louis-Napoleon president and was an empire again within four years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1848).

name: The Communist Manifesto
summary: Marx and Engels published a short pamphlet arguing that history is driven by class struggle.
body:
*The Communist Manifesto* is a short pamphlet by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, published in London in February 1848 as the programme of the Communist League. It argues that the history of society is the history of class struggle, that industrial capitalism has reduced that struggle to two classes, and that the working class will overthrow the bourgeoisie and abolish private property in the means of production.

It is a political text rather than an analysis: about thirty pages, written to be read aloud, ending in a call for the workers of all countries to unite. Marx's economic argument came later and at length, in *Capital*. The pamphlet appeared weeks before the [revolutions of 1848](event:revolutions-1848) began and had almost no effect on them; it was rediscovered in the 1870s and translated widely thereafter.

It became the founding document of the socialist and communist movements, and the states that took power in its name, after the [Russian Revolution](event:russian-revolution) and later in [China](event:prc-founded) and elsewhere, governed roughly a third of the world's population for much of the twentieth century. It remains one of the most widely printed political works ever written.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto).

name: Taiping Rebellion
summary: A millenarian movement led by a man who believed he was Jesus's younger brother held southern China for a decade; 20–30 million died.
body:
Part of the [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). The Taiping Rebellion was a civil war in southern China from 1850 to 1864, fought between the [Qing](event:qing-dynasty) government and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, a millenarian Christian movement led by Hong Xiuquan, who believed himself the younger brother of Jesus. Estimates of the dead run from 20 to 30 million, which makes it one of the deadliest wars in history.

Hong's movement grew out of the Hakka communities of Guangxi among people impoverished and displaced after the [Opium War](event:opium-wars). It combined a radical religious programme with land redistribution, the abolition of foot-binding, opium and concubinage, and a strict separation of the sexes. The Taiping took Nanjing in 1853 and held it as their capital for eleven years, ruling much of the Yangtze valley.

The Qing could not defeat them with the regular banner armies and had to rely on provincial forces raised by officials such as Zeng Guofan, with foreign-officered units in the coastal region late in the war. Nanjing fell in 1864 after a long siege. The war depopulated some of the richest provinces in China, cost the dynasty its finances and much of its authority, and shifted military power to the provincial armies, where it remained after the dynasty fell.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiping_Rebellion).

name: Crimean War
summary: Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire fought Russia over influence in the Black Sea and the Holy Land, and over the fate of a declining Ottoman Empire.
body:
The Crimean War was fought from 1853 to 1856 between Russia on one side and the Ottoman Empire, France, Britain and Sardinia on the other. It began over the protection of Christians in the Ottoman lands and over influence in the Black Sea, and it was decided by a year-long siege of the Russian naval base at Sevastopol. Russia lost.

Most of the fighting took place on the Crimean peninsula after the allies landed there in September 1854: the battles of the Alma, Balaclava and Inkerman, and then the siege. Both sides were badly supplied and badly led; far more men died of cholera, typhus and dysentery than of wounds. The war produced the first war correspondents filing by [telegraph](event:telegraph) and the first widely seen war photographs, and the reporting of the state of the hospitals brought Florence Nightingale to Scutari and led to the reform of military nursing and sanitation.

The Treaty of Paris of 1856 neutralised the Black Sea, terms Russia repudiated as soon as the other powers were distracted in 1870. Defeat exposed how far Russia had fallen behind industrially and pushed St Petersburg into the reforms that ended serfdom in 1861. It also broke the concert of great powers that had held since 1815 and left Austria isolated.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War).

name: Bessemer steel process
summary: Henry Bessemer's process converted pig iron to steel in bulk, cutting costs and making railroads and armaments much cheaper.
body:
Part of [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution). The Bessemer process, patented by Henry Bessemer in 1856, made steel a bulk material for the first time. Air blown through a converter full of molten pig iron burns out the carbon and silicon, and the heat of that reaction keeps the metal liquid without extra fuel. A charge of several tonnes could be converted in about twenty minutes, where the older crucible and puddling methods took a day and produced far less.

The price of steel fell by roughly an order of magnitude within a generation. The first converters produced brittle metal from phosphoric ores, which was solved by Robert Mushet's addition of spiegeleisen and later by the Gilchrist-Thomas basic lining; the open-hearth process then took much of the market because it could use scrap and was easier to control.

Cheap steel replaced iron in rails, which had worn out under heavy traffic, and so made the great trunk and [transcontinental lines](event:transcontinental-railroad) practical. It also went into ship hulls, bridges, boilers, framed buildings, armour plate and artillery, and it underwrote the naval arms race that preceded [World War I](event:ww1). It is the usual marker of the second phase of the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessemer_process).

name: Indian Rebellion
summary: Indian soldiers and civilians rose against the East India Company in 1857; the rebellion took over a year to suppress and ended Company rule.
body:
Part of the [East India Company](event:english-east-india) era in India. The Indian Rebellion of 1857 was a large uprising against the rule of the [East India Company](event:english-east-india) in northern and central India. It began as a mutiny of the Company's own Indian soldiers at Meerut in May 1857 and spread into a civil rebellion joined by dispossessed princes, landholders and peasants. It took the British more than a year to suppress.

The immediate trigger was the new Enfield rifle, whose cartridges were rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat and had to be bitten open, which offended Hindu and Muslim soldiers alike. Behind it lay annexations under the doctrine of lapse, the displacement of Indian rulers and landholders, revenue settlements that ruined cultivators, and fear of interference with religion. The rebels took Delhi and proclaimed the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, as their sovereign; Kanpur and Lucknow were besieged.

Both sides killed prisoners and civilians, and British reprisals after the recapture of the cities included mass executions, some carried out in public by blowing men from guns, and the burning of villages. Hundreds of thousands died, the great majority of them Indian. The Government of India Act of 1858 abolished the Company and transferred its territory and army to the Crown, beginning the [British Raj](event:british-raj); the army was reorganised with a far higher proportion of British troops, and the promise not to interfere in religion was made explicit.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Rebellion_of_1857).

name: First transatlantic telegraph cable
summary: A submarine telegraph cable successfully crossed the Atlantic, connecting North America to Europe and shortening communication from ten days to minutes.
body:
Part of [Electric telegraph](event:telegraph). The first telegraph cable across the Atlantic was completed in August 1858, linking Valentia Island in Ireland to Trinity Bay in Newfoundland. It worked for about three weeks, long enough to carry congratulations between Queen Victoria and President Buchanan at some hours per message, and then failed. A durable cable was laid in 1866 by the *Great Eastern*, which also recovered and completed the broken cable of the previous year.

The engineering problems were new at every scale: manufacturing and coiling more than 3,000 kilometres of cable, paying it out over deep water without snapping it, and detecting a signal so attenuated by the long line that ordinary instruments could not read it. William Thomson's mirror galvanometer solved the last of these; the 1858 cable had been ruined by applying high voltages in an attempt to force a signal through it.

A message from London to New York had taken about ten days by ship and now took minutes. Financial markets on the two sides of the ocean began to move together, news travelled ahead of the ships that carried it, and within two decades submarine cables linked most of the world's ports into one system.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transatlantic_telegraph_cable).

name: British Raj
summary: The Crown took over direct rule of India from the East India Company after the rebellion of 1857.
body:
The British Raj was the rule of the British Crown over the Indian subcontinent from 1858 to 1947. It replaced the [East India Company](event:english-east-india), whose territories and army were transferred to the Crown after the [rebellion of 1857](event:indian-rebellion), and covered present-day India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, together with several hundred nominally independent princely states.

A small British civil service and an army with a large Indian rank and file governed some 300 million people. The period brought railways, telegraph lines, canal irrigation, a codified legal system and English-language universities. It also brought a revenue system that pressed hard on cultivators, tariff and trade policy that favoured British manufactures over Indian ones, and a series of famines (1876–78, 1896–97 and Bengal in 1943) in which millions died. The administration's response to the famines is a central subject of debate about the period.

Organised nationalism grew from the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885, through the [Salt March](event:salt-march) and the [Quit India](event:quit-india) movement led by [Gandhi](item:mohandas-gandhi), to the post-war Labour government's decision to transfer power. The Raj ended in August 1947 with [independence and partition](event:indian-independence), which displaced perhaps fifteen million people and killed several hundred thousand.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj).

name: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
summary: Darwin set out the theory that species descend with modification from common ancestors through natural selection.
body:
*On the Origin of Species* was published in London on 24 November 1859. In it [Charles Darwin](item:charles-darwin) argued that species are not fixed but descend with modification from common ancestors, and that the process producing them is [natural selection](item:natural-selection): heritable variation, more offspring than can survive, and the differential survival that follows. The first printing of 1,250 copies sold out at once.

Darwin had held the argument back for twenty years and published only when Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay from the Malay Archipelago reaching the same conclusion. The book itself is a long accumulation of evidence from domestic breeding, the fossil record, geographical distribution, embryology and rudimentary organs, presented as one argument rather than as a set of proofs, and it deals openly with the objections Darwin could not answer.

The weakest point was heredity: Darwin had no mechanism for how variation was passed on or preserved, and blending inheritance would have destroyed it. That gap closed only when Mendelian genetics was joined to selection in the modern synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s, and again with the [structure of DNA](event:dna-structure). Common descent was accepted by biologists within a decade or two; natural selection as the main mechanism took much longer. The book is the founding work of evolutionary biology. Opposition to it continued, including at the [Scopes trial](event:scopes-trial) in 1925.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Origin_of_Species).

name: Evolution by natural selection
summary: The explanation of adaptation without design: heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction, repeated over generations.
body:
Natural selection is the process that produces adaptation without a designer. Where organisms vary, where some of that variation is inherited, and where more offspring are produced than can survive, the variants that leave more descendants become more common. Repeated over many generations, this shapes populations in ways that look designed.

The argument has three premises and one conclusion, and each premise is an observation rather than an assumption. [Darwin](item:charles-darwin) and Alfred Russel Wallace arrived at it independently and published jointly in 1858; [*On the Origin of Species*](item:origin-species) set out the evidence the following year.

Its weakest point was heredity, for which Darwin had no mechanism, and it was resolved only when Mendelian genetics was combined with selection in the modern synthesis of the 1930s and 40s, and again by the [structure of DNA](item:dna-structure) and the reading of [whole genomes](item:human-genome).

Natural selection is not the only evolutionary process: drift, migration and mutation all change populations, and much molecular change is effectively neutral. It is, however, the only known process that produces adaptation, and it applies wherever there is heritable variation in reproductive success, including bacteria acquiring antibiotic resistance and viruses evolving during an epidemic.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_selection).

name: Germ theory established
summary: Pasteur, Koch and Lister established that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.
body:
Between about 1860 and 1885 a handful of researchers established that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases. Louis Pasteur showed that fermentation and putrefaction are the work of living organisms and that they do not arise spontaneously; Robert Koch isolated the bacilli of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera and set out the criteria for proving that one organism causes one disease; Joseph Lister applied the inference to surgery.

Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments of 1859–61 removed the last serious defence of spontaneous generation. Lister introduced carbolic antisepsis at Glasgow in 1867 and cut mortality after amputation sharply. Koch's postulates, formulated in the 1880s, gave the field a method rather than a set of anecdotes, and the identification of one pathogen after another followed within a few years. Pasteur's rabies vaccine of 1885 showed that the [theory](item:germ-theory-of-disease) could be turned back on the disease.

The practical consequences arrived long before there was much to treat infection with: sterile surgery, safe water, sewerage, food hygiene and pasteurisation. Together with [vaccination](event:smallpox-vaccine) and later [antibiotics](event:penicillin) they are the main reason human life expectancy roughly doubled over the following century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_theory_of_disease).

name: Germ theory of disease
summary: The principle that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases, displacing miasma and imbalance as explanations of illness.
body:
The germ theory of disease is the principle that many illnesses are caused by microorganisms that invade the body, and that a particular organism causes a particular disease. It displaced explanations in terms of bad air, imbalance of humours and divine punishment, and it is the foundation of modern medicine and public health.

For most of history epidemics were explained by miasma, imbalance or punishment. Microorganisms had been visible since [Leeuwenhoek's microscopes](item:leeuwenhoek-microscope) in the 1670s, but nothing connected them to illness until the nineteenth century.

The case was assembled piece by piece: John Snow traced a cholera outbreak to a single London water pump in 1854; Pasteur showed that fermentation and putrefaction are the work of living organisms and that heating kills them; Lister applied the inference to surgery with carbolic antisepsis; Robert Koch isolated the anthrax and tuberculosis bacilli and set out the postulates that establish which organism causes which disease.

Sterile surgery, safe water, sewerage and food hygiene cut mortality long before there was much to treat infections with, and the theory made [vaccination](item:smallpox-vaccine) intelligible rather than merely empirical and [antibiotics](item:penicillin) conceivable. Retrospective diagnosis of past epidemics such as the [Black Death](item:black-death) and the [Plague of Justinian](item:justinian-plague) rests on it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germ_theory_of_disease).

name: American Civil War
summary: Eleven southern states seceded to preserve slavery; four years of war ended slavery and cost some 700,000 lives.
body:
The American Civil War was fought from April 1861 to the spring of 1865 between the United States (the Union) and the Confederate States, eleven southern states that had seceded after the election of [Abraham Lincoln](item:abraham-lincoln). The Confederacy was defeated, secession was ended, and slavery was abolished throughout the country. About 700,000 soldiers died, more Americans than in any other war.

Slavery was the cause. The Confederate states seceded to protect an institution that held four million people, and said so in their declarations of secession; the immediate trigger was the election of a president committed to keeping slavery out of the western territories. Lincoln's war aim at the start was the restoration of the Union rather than abolition, which was what held the slaveholding border states in it.

The North had four times the free population, most of the industry, most of the railways and a navy. The South had to defend rather than conquer, had better field commanders in the east for the first two years, and hoped that European powers dependent on its cotton would intervene. Union strategy settled into blockade of the coast, control of the Mississippi to split the Confederacy in two, and pressure on the Confederate armies in Virginia and Tennessee at once.

The [Emancipation Proclamation](event:emancipation) of 1863 turned the war into a war against slavery, made European recognition of the Confederacy politically impossible, and brought some 180,000 black soldiers and sailors into Union service. In 1864 Grant took command in the east and fought Lee continuously rather than in separate campaigns, while Sherman took Atlanta and marched to the sea, destroying the resources the Confederate armies lived on.

Lee surrendered at Appomattox on 9 April 1865 and the remaining Confederate forces gave up over the following weeks. Lincoln was [assassinated](event:lincoln-assassination) five days after Appomattox. The Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments abolished slavery and wrote citizenship and voting rights into the constitution; the Reconstruction that was to enforce them was abandoned by 1877, and the South imposed segregation and disenfranchisement that lasted until the [civil rights movement](event:civil-rights).

The war's course is followed in the steps below.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War).

steps.name: Fort Sumter
steps.page:
Confederate batteries opened fire on the Federal garrison of Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour on 12 April 1861, after Lincoln announced that he would resupply it. The fort surrendered the next day; nobody was killed in the bombardment.

Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to suppress the rebellion, and four more states (Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina) seceded rather than furnish troops against their neighbours.

steps.name: First Bull Run
steps.page:
The first large battle was fought on 21 July 1861 beside a stream called Bull Run, thirty miles from Washington, between armies of ninety-day volunteers watched by spectators who had driven out from the capital.

The Union attack broke up in confusion and the retreat became a rout. It ended the expectation on both sides that the war would be settled in a single campaign, and the Union began raising and training armies for a long one.

steps.name: Antietam
steps.page:
Lee invaded Maryland in September 1862 and was met at Antietam Creek on the 17th. Around 22,000 men were killed, wounded or missing in a single day, the bloodiest day in American history.

The battle was tactically inconclusive but Lee withdrew into Virginia, which was enough of a victory for Lincoln to announce the preliminary [Emancipation Proclamation](item:emancipation) five days later, and enough to end any prospect of British or French recognition of the Confederacy.

steps.name: Vicksburg
steps.page:
Vicksburg on its bluff was the last Confederate stronghold on the Mississippi. Grant crossed the river below it, marched inland away from his supply line, beat the forces in his way and then besieged the city from the land side for six weeks.

The garrison of about 30,000 surrendered on 4 July 1863, the day after [Gettysburg](item:gettysburg). The Union now held the river along its whole length, and the Confederacy was cut in two.

steps.name: Sherman's March to the Sea
steps.page:
After taking Atlanta in September 1864, a victory that helped re-elect Lincoln in November, Sherman cut loose from his supply line and marched 60,000 men across Georgia to Savannah, which he reached three days before Christmas.

His army lived off the country and destroyed railways, mills, cotton and food stores as it went. The march was directed at the will and the means to continue the war rather than at an opposing army, and Sherman turned north into the Carolinas to repeat it.

steps.name: Appomattox
steps.page:
Grant's Overland Campaign of 1864 cost enormous casualties and pinned Lee at Petersburg through a nine-month siege. When the line broke on 2 April 1865 Richmond was abandoned and burned, and Lee's army marched west with the Union cavalry ahead of it.

Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia at Appomattox Court House on 9 April. The terms let his men go home with their horses, and the pattern was followed by the surrenders that ended the war elsewhere over the following seven weeks.

name: Emancipation Proclamation
summary: Lincoln declared enslaved people in the rebelling states to be free; the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery outright in 1865.
body:
Part of [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war). The Emancipation Proclamation was an executive order issued by [Abraham Lincoln](item:abraham-lincoln) on 1 January 1863, declaring free all people held as slaves in the states then in rebellion. It applied to about three and a half million people. Lincoln had announced it in preliminary form the previous September, after the battle of Antietam gave him a victory to announce it from.

It was framed as a war measure taken under the president's authority as commander-in-chief, which is why it reached only the rebelling states: the loyal slaveholding border states and areas already under Union control were exempt, and about 800,000 people were left in slavery by it. Where the Union army advanced, it freed people in fact as well as in law, and the proclamation also opened enlistment, bringing some 180,000 black soldiers and sailors into Union service.

Its effect was to change what the war was about. A war for the restoration of the Union became a war against slavery, which made European recognition of the Confederacy politically impossible and ruled out any negotiated peace that left slavery standing. Slavery itself was abolished throughout the United States by the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation).

name: Battle of Gettysburg
summary: Three days of fighting in Pennsylvania ended Lee's invasion of the North.
body:
Part of [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war). The Battle of Gettysburg was fought on 1–3 July 1863 around a small town in southern Pennsylvania. Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia, invading the North for the second time, met George Meade's Army of the Potomac and was beaten. With about 50,000 killed, wounded, captured or missing on the two sides, it was the costliest battle of the [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war).

The armies collided by accident west of the town on the first day and the Confederates drove the Union forces back through it onto the high ground to the south. That ground decided the battle: the Union line held Cemetery Hill, Culp's Hill and the ridge running south to Little Round Top, and the Confederate attacks on both flanks on the second day failed to take it. On the third day Lee sent about 12,000 men across open ground against the Union centre, an attack known as Pickett's Charge, and lost more than half of them in an hour.

Lee withdrew into Virginia and never mounted another invasion of the North; Vicksburg surrendered in the west the next day. In November, at the dedication of the soldiers' cemetery, Lincoln gave a two-minute address restating the war as a test of whether a nation conceived in liberty could endure.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gettysburg).

name: Assassination of Abraham Lincoln
summary: Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre five days after Lee's surrender.
body:
Part of [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war). [Abraham Lincoln](item:abraham-lincoln) was shot at Ford's Theatre in Washington on the evening of 14 April 1865 and died the next morning. The killer was John Wilkes Booth, a well-known actor and Confederate sympathiser. It was five days after Lee's surrender at Appomattox, and Lincoln was the first American president to be assassinated.

Booth walked into the unguarded presidential box during a performance of *Our American Cousin*, fired a single shot into the back of Lincoln's head, and escaped across the stage. The attack was part of a conspiracy meant to decapitate the Union government: an accomplice stabbed and badly wounded the Secretary of State, William Seward, the same night, and a third man assigned to the Vice-President lost his nerve. Booth was cornered in a Virginia barn twelve days later and shot; four of the conspirators were hanged in July.

Lincoln's death removed the one figure with the authority and the inclination to press a moderate Reconstruction. His successor, Andrew Johnson, quarrelled with Congress over the terms and was impeached; the political settlement that followed left the freed population of the South without the protection Lincoln had begun to argue for.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln).

name: Marie Curie
summary: Polish-French physicist and chemist who discovered polonium and radium, coined the term radioactivity, and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences.
body:
Marie Curie (1867–1934) was a Polish-French physicist and chemist who established that radiation can come from inside the atom, named the phenomenon radioactivity, and discovered the elements polonium and radium. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and remains the only person to have won one in two different sciences.

Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw under Russian rule, she was barred as a woman from the university there and studied instead at the clandestine Flying University before leaving for Paris in 1891. At the Sorbonne she took degrees in physics and mathematics, and in 1895 married Pierre Curie.

Following Henri Becquerel's discovery that uranium salts emit [radiation of their own accord](item:radioactivity), she measured the effect in every element she could obtain, showed that it came from the atom itself, and named it radioactivity. Processing tonnes of pitchblende by hand, the Curies isolated two new elements in 1898: polonium, named for her homeland, and radium. She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Becquerel, and took the 1911 Prize in Chemistry alone.

During [the First World War](item:ww1) she equipped mobile radiological units (the *petites Curies*) and trained their operators, bringing [X-ray](item:x-rays) diagnosis to the front. She died of aplastic anaemia, attributed to her long exposure to radiation; her notebooks remain radioactive.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie).

name: Meiji Restoration
summary: Japan abolished the shogunate and deliberately industrialised, becoming a great power within a generation.
body:
The Meiji Restoration was the transfer of political power in Japan from the Tokugawa shogunate back to the emperor, proclaimed in January 1868. The new government then set out deliberately to remake the country on Western industrial and military lines, and did so fast enough that Japan was recognised as a great power within forty years.

The shogunate had been discredited by its inability to resist the foreign warships that [ended Japan's seclusion](event:edo-japan) in the 1850s and by the unequal treaties it signed. Domains in the south-west, chiefly Satsuma and Chōshū, overthrew it in a short civil war and governed in the young Meiji emperor's name from Tokyo.

The reforms were radical and quick. The domains were abolished and replaced by prefectures; the samurai lost their stipends, their swords and their monopoly of arms to a conscript army; land tax was put on a money basis; and railways, telegraphs, shipyards, banks, factories and a national school system were built, often by the state and then sold to private owners. Missions were sent abroad to study foreign institutions, and a constitution and elected Diet followed in 1889–90. Rapid industrialisation was paid for largely by the countryside, and it came with an expansionist foreign policy that produced victory over China in 1895 and over [Russia](event:russo-japanese-war) in 1905.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Restoration).

name: Suez Canal opens
summary: A sea-level canal between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea cut thousands of kilometres from the Europe–Asia route.
body:
The Suez Canal opened on 17 November 1869. It runs about 164 kilometres across the Isthmus of Suez between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, at sea level and without locks, and it removed the need to sail around Africa to reach Asia from Europe. The route from London to Bombay was shortened by roughly 7,000 kilometres.

The canal was built by Ferdinand de Lesseps' Suez Canal Company under a concession from the Egyptian viceroy. Much of the early excavation was done by conscripted Egyptian labour under the corvée, with heavy loss of life, before dredgers and mechanical excavators took over. The cost helped bankrupt the Egyptian state, and in 1875 Britain bought its shares in the company; British troops occupied Egypt in 1882, largely to secure the waterway.

The canal made steamships economic on the Asian routes, since a steamer could refuel at ports along the way where a sailing ship needed the winds of the Cape. It became the main route for oil from the Gulf, and its nationalisation in 1956 led to the [Suez Crisis](event:suez-crisis).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Canal).

name: First transcontinental railroad
summary: The golden spike at Promontory Summit joined the American rail network coast to coast.
body:
Part of [First passenger railway](event:railways). The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on 10 May 1869, when a ceremonial golden spike was driven at Promontory Summit in Utah. It joined the Central Pacific, built eastward from Sacramento, to the Union Pacific, built westward from the Missouri River, and connected the existing eastern network to the Pacific coast.

The line was authorised during the [Civil War](event:us-civil-war) and paid for with federal land grants and loans, which made the race between the two companies a race for subsidy. The Central Pacific's hardest work was the crossing of the Sierra Nevada, where tunnels were cut through granite by hand and by blasting powder, largely by Chinese labourers who made up most of its workforce; the Union Pacific, laying track fast across the plains, employed many Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans.

A journey that had taken four to six months by wagon or ship now took about a week. The railroad opened the interior to settlement and to commercial agriculture, carried cattle and grain to eastern markets, and hastened the destruction of the Plains nations' economy, which rested on bison herds the line cut through. It is the standard example of what [railways](event:railways) did to the scale of a continent.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_transcontinental_railroad).

name: Mendeleev's periodic table
summary: Arranging the elements by weight and property revealed a periodic law, and gaps where undiscovered elements had to be.
body:
In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known chemical elements in order of atomic weight and found that their properties repeat at regular intervals. Setting elements with similar properties beneath one another produced the periodic table, which remains the organising diagram of chemistry.

Others had noticed partial regularities: Döbereiner's triads, Newlands' octaves, and Lothar Meyer's nearly simultaneous table. What made Mendeleev's version decisive was his willingness to trust the pattern over the data: where an element did not fit, he left a gap rather than closing the row, and where a measured weight contradicted the periodicity, he argued that the measurement was wrong. He predicted the properties of three missing elements in detail, and gallium, scandium and germanium were found between 1875 and 1886 close to specification.

The reason for the periodicity was not known until atomic structure was understood. Henry Moseley showed in 1913 that the correct ordering is by nuclear charge rather than by weight, which removed the remaining anomalies, and quantum mechanics later explained the rows and columns as the filling of electron shells. The table has since been extended by the noble gases, the lanthanides and actinides, and the synthetic elements beyond uranium.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table).

name: Mohandas Gandhi
summary: Leader of the Indian independence movement, who made non-violent mass civil disobedience an instrument of political change.
body:
Mohandas Gandhi (1869–1948) led the Indian independence movement and made organised non-violent civil disobedience an instrument of mass politics. He turned the Indian National Congress into a movement with a popular base, and his methods were studied and copied by campaigns for civil rights and against colonial rule across the world.

Gandhi trained as a barrister in London and spent twenty years in South Africa, where discrimination against Indian residents led him to develop *satyagraha*, a form of non-violent resistance in which participants openly refuse to comply with a law and accept the penalty for it.

Returning to India in 1915, he organised peasants and mill workers, launched non-cooperation with [British rule](item:british-raj), and in 1930 walked 385 kilometres to the sea to make salt in defiance of the government monopoly; the [Salt March](item:salt-march) drew tens of thousands into civil disobedience. The [Quit India](item:quit-india) movement of 1942 brought him and most of the Congress leadership to prison.

He campaigned against untouchability and for Hindu-Muslim unity, and opposed [the partition](item:partition) that accompanied [independence](item:indian-independence) in 1947. He was shot in Delhi in January 1948 by a Hindu nationalist who thought him too conciliatory towards Muslims. His methods were studied closely by later movements, among them the [American civil rights campaign](item:civil-rights).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi).

name: Metre Convention standardises metric system
summary: Seventeen nations agreed on standard definitions of the metre and kilogram, making the metric system international.
body:
The Metre Convention was signed in Paris on 20 May 1875 by seventeen states. It made the metric system an international rather than a French affair: the signatories agreed to share physical standards for the metre and the kilogram, and created permanent institutions to keep and compare them.

France had built the metric system during the [Revolution](event:french-revolution), defining the metre as a fraction of the earth's meridian, but for decades it spread slowly and Britain and the United States kept their own units. The convention set up the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sèvres outside Paris, together with a general conference and a committee to govern it. Prototype bars and cylinders of platinum-iridium were manufactured and distributed to the member states in 1889.

The definitions have since been rebuilt on physical constants rather than artefacts: the metre in terms of the speed of light in 1983, and in 2019 the kilogram in terms of the Planck constant, which retired the last object serving as a standard. The system the convention created became the International System of Units, the legal basis of measurement in almost every country and the common language of science and trade.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_Convention).

name: Telephone
summary: Alexander Graham Bell patented a device that carried the human voice over a wire.
body:
Alexander Graham Bell was granted a United States patent for the telephone on 7 March 1876, and made the first intelligible transmission of speech over a wire three days later. Where the [telegraph](event:telegraph) carried coded pulses that a trained operator had to translate at each end, the telephone carried the voice itself, and could be used by anyone.

The principle is that sound vibrations move a membrane, the membrane varies an electric current, and at the far end the varying current moves another membrane. Several people were working on it: Elisha Gray filed a caveat describing a liquid transmitter on the same day as Bell's patent application, and the priority dispute has been argued ever since; Antonio Meucci had demonstrated a voice-carrying device years earlier without being able to afford a patent.

The Bell Telephone Company was formed in 1877, and exchanges spread quickly through American and European cities, since switching allowed any subscriber to reach any other without a dedicated line. The telephone changed business, journalism and domestic life, and the networks built for it (copper pairs, exchanges and long-distance trunks) later carried the first data traffic of the [internet](event:internet).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone).

name: Edison's phonograph
summary: Thomas Edison built the first device that could both record sound and play it back, capturing a voice on a cylinder wrapped in tinfoil.
body:
Thomas Edison built the phonograph in 1877, the first device that could both record sound and play it back. A stylus cut a groove into tinfoil wrapped on a rotating cylinder as a diaphragm vibrated; running the stylus back along the groove reproduced the sound. Édouard-Léon Scott had recorded sound waves twenty years earlier, but had no way to hear them again.

The first recording Edison made was of himself reciting "Mary Had a Little Lamb". Early cylinders were fragile, quiet and hard to duplicate, and Edison first advertised the machine as a dictation device. Emile Berliner's gramophone of 1887 used a flat disc that could be stamped in quantity, and by the early twentieth century the disc had won the market.

Recording separated a performance from the moment and place it happened. A commercial music industry followed, built on selling copies rather than tickets; performers could reach audiences they never met, and could outlast themselves. Recorded sound also gave linguists and ethnographers a way to preserve speech and music, and the engineering problem of reproducing it faithfully shaped radio broadcasting and [sound film](event:jazz-singer).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph).

name: Practical electric lighting
summary: Edison's long-lasting incandescent lamp, and the generating stations built to supply it, electrified cities.
body:
In 1879 Thomas Edison demonstrated an incandescent lamp with a carbon filament in an evacuated glass bulb that burned for many hours at a practical cost. Joseph Swan had shown a similar lamp in Britain at about the same time, and the two later merged their British interests. Electric light in the home dates from this work.

The bulb was the smaller half of the problem. Edison's laboratory at Menlo Park designed a whole system around it: a generating station, distribution mains, meters, fuses, sockets and switches, and a lamp with high enough resistance to let many be run in parallel from one supply without enormous copper. The Pearl Street Station in Manhattan began supplying customers in September 1882.

Electric lighting displaced gas within a generation in the cities that could afford it. It was clean, did not consume the air of a room, and reduced the fire risk that had shaped theatres, factories and warehouses; it also decoupled working and social hours from daylight. The generating and distribution networks built to sell light then became the electrical supply that ran motors, trams, appliances and eventually everything else.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incandescent_light_bulb).

name: Albert Einstein
summary: Theoretical physicist whose work on relativity, light quanta and statistical mechanics changed the physics of space, time, matter and energy.
body:
Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a theoretical physicist whose work reorganised the physics of space, time, matter and energy. [Special relativity](item:relativity) abandoned absolute time, general relativity replaced gravitational force with the curvature of spacetime, and his paper on light quanta was one of the founding documents of quantum theory. He is widely regarded as one of the most influential scientists of the twentieth century.

Einstein was born at Ulm and educated in Munich, Aarau and Zurich. Unable to find an academic post, he took work at the Swiss patent office in Bern, and in 1905, his *annus mirabilis*, published four papers in a single year: on the photoelectric effect, on Brownian motion, on the electrodynamics of moving bodies, and on the equivalence of mass and energy.

Ten years later general relativity recast gravity as geometry; the bending of starlight measured during the 1919 eclipse made him famous outside physics. The theory's later predictions include black holes and [gravitational waves](item:gravitational-waves), detected a century after he wrote it down. See also the article on [relativity](item:theory-of-relativity).

He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for the photoelectric effect rather than for relativity. A Jewish pacifist, he left Germany when [Hitler took power](item:hitler-chancellor) and settled at Princeton, where he spent his last two decades on an unsuccessful search for a unified field theory and in public argument against militarism and racial segregation. In 1939 he signed a letter to President Roosevelt warning that [nuclear fission](item:nuclear-fission) might make a bomb possible. He later described the letter as his one great mistake.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein).

name: Modern global warming
summary: Greenhouse gases released since the Industrial Revolution have warmed the planet by about 1.3 °C, and the rate is increasing.
body:
Modern global warming is the rise in the earth's surface temperature caused by greenhouse gases released by human activity, chiefly carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels. The global average is now about 1.3 °C above the late-nineteenth-century baseline, and the warming is continuing.

The physics has been understood for a long time. Fourier described the atmosphere's heat-trapping effect in the 1820s, Tyndall measured which gases do it in the 1850s, and Arrhenius calculated in 1896 roughly how much warming a doubling of carbon dioxide would produce. Continuous measurement of atmospheric CO2 began at Mauna Loa in 1958 and has risen every year since, from about 280 parts per million before the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution) to over 420 today.

The observed consequences include the loss of mass from ice sheets and mountain glaciers, sea level rise of over 20 centimetres since 1900 and accelerating, ocean acidification, shifts in the ranges of species, and a measurable increase in the frequency and intensity of extreme heat. Attribution studies now link individual heatwaves and floods to the warming with quantified confidence.

The international response runs through the framework convention of 1992, the [Kyoto Protocol](event:kyoto-protocol) and the [Paris Agreement](event:paris-agreement) of 2015, which aims to hold warming well below 2 °C. Emissions have not yet peaked. The closest geological analogue for a rapid carbon release is the [PETM](event:petm), 56 million years ago, which was far slower.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming).

name: Scramble for Africa
summary: European powers partitioned almost the entire African continent among themselves in three decades.
body:
The Scramble for Africa was the conquest, occupation and division of almost the whole African continent by European powers between about 1881 and 1914. At the start of the period Europeans held coastal enclaves and a few colonies; at the end, only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent. Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Portugal, Italy and Spain divided the rest.

The causes were mixed: competition for raw materials and markets in an industrialising Europe, rivalry between the powers for prestige and strategic position, missionary and abolitionist pressure, and the technical means to act on any of it. Quinine prophylaxis, steamboats on the rivers, the [telegraph](event:telegraph) and breech-loading and then machine guns turned expeditions that had previously failed into ones that succeeded cheaply.

Resistance was widespread, took every form from diplomacy to conventional war, and was occasionally successful; but it was generally broken by force. Famine, forced labour and punitive expeditions cost millions of lives. The steps below follow the partition from the occupation of Egypt to the German war in South West Africa.

The borders drawn in this period cut across languages, states and trading systems, and they are largely the borders of Africa today. The colonial administrations they created lasted until [decolonisation](event:decolonisation) after 1945.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scramble_for_Africa).

steps.name: The occupation of Egypt
steps.page:
Egypt had borrowed heavily to build the [Suez Canal](item:suez-canal) and to modernise, and went bankrupt in 1876; British and French controllers took charge of its finances, and a nationalist movement in the army rose against them.

Britain bombarded Alexandria in July 1882 and destroyed the Egyptian army at Tel el-Kebir on 13 September. The occupation was announced as temporary and lasted, in one form or another, until 1956. It gave Britain the canal, the Nile and a reason to push south into the Sudan, and it made the other powers move on claims of their own.

steps.name: The Berlin Conference
steps.page:
Fourteen states met in Berlin between November 1884 and February 1885, at Bismarck's invitation, to agree rules for their claims in Africa. No African ruler was present or represented.

The General Act declared free navigation on the Congo and Niger, condemned the slave trade, and required a power claiming a coast to occupy it effectively and to notify the others. It did not itself partition the continent, but it turned the claiming of it into a procedure, and the pace of annexation rose sharply afterwards.
