steps.name: The Congo Free State
steps.page:
The conference recognised the Congo basin as the personal property of Leopold II of Belgium, who had assembled it through a philanthropic association and Henry Morton Stanley's expeditions. It was a state of about 2.3 million square kilometres owned by one man.

Its revenue came from ivory and then from wild rubber, collected under quotas enforced by an armed militia through hostage-taking, flogging and the severing of hands. Missionary and consular reporting, including Roger Casement's report of 1904 and E. D. Morel's campaign, made the territory an international scandal, and Belgium annexed the territory from its king in 1908. Estimates of the population loss run into millions.

steps.name: Adwa
steps.page:
Italy claimed a protectorate over Ethiopia on the strength of a disputed clause in the Treaty of Wuchale, and invaded from Eritrea. Menelik II met the invading force at Adwa on 1 March 1896 with an army several times its size, well armed with rifles and artillery bought from Europe.

The Italian army was destroyed. Ethiopia's independence was recognised by treaty, and it remained, with Liberia, one of the two African states outside European rule until Italy [invaded in 1935](item:abyssinia-invasion).

steps.name: Fashoda
steps.page:
A small French expedition under Jean-Baptiste Marchand marched across Africa from the Atlantic and reached the Nile at Fashoda in July 1898, intending to make good a French line of claim from west to east. Kitchener arrived from the north with a far larger force in September, having just destroyed the Mahdist state at Omdurman.

The two commanders avoided a clash on the spot, but for weeks the two powers were close to war before France withdrew. The settlement that followed left Britain the Nile valley and France a belt across west and central Africa, and began the rapprochement that became the Entente Cordiale.

steps.name: The Herero and Nama genocide
steps.page:
The Herero of German South West Africa rose against settler expropriation in January 1904. After defeating them at the Waterberg in August, Lothar von Trotha issued an order that any Herero found in the territory would be shot, and drove the survivors into the Omaheke desert, where the water holes were guarded.

The Nama rose the following year and were treated the same way. Survivors were held in camps at Shark Island and elsewhere, where most died of exhaustion and disease. Perhaps 80 per cent of the Herero and half the Nama were killed. It is generally described as the first genocide of the twentieth century, and Germany formally acknowledged it as such in 2021.

name: Eruption of Krakatoa
summary: The explosion was heard 4,800 km away and the tsunamis it raised killed more than 36,000 people.
body:
Krakatoa, a volcanic island in the strait between Java and Sumatra, destroyed itself in a series of eruptions on 26 and 27 August 1883. The final explosions were heard nearly 5,000 kilometres away in Australia and on Rodrigues in the Indian Ocean, one of the loudest sounds ever recorded, and the pressure wave was registered by barographs around the world several times as it circled the earth.

Most of the dead were killed not by the eruption but by the tsunamis it raised, some over 30 metres high, which swept the coasts of Java and Sumatra and destroyed 165 villages. The official Dutch colonial count was 36,417 dead. Ash fell over an enormous area and the sea for hundreds of kilometres around was covered with floating pumice.

Sulphate injected into the stratosphere lowered global average temperatures by roughly half a degree for several years and produced vivid sunsets and a bluish moon in Europe and North America for months. Because submarine cables and the [telegraph](event:telegraph) were by then in place, Krakatoa was the first natural disaster on this scale to be reported around the world within hours, and it was studied internationally almost at once.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1883_eruption_of_Krakatoa).

name: Kodak roll film camera
summary: George Eastman produced the first roll-film camera cheap enough for amateurs, and photography spread beyond professionals.
body:
In 1888 George Eastman put on sale the Kodak, a simple box camera loaded with a roll of flexible film. It cost $25, came ready-loaded with enough film for a hundred exposures, and was sold with the slogan "You press the button, we do the rest": the whole camera went back to the factory, which developed the pictures and returned it reloaded.

Photography before this required glass plates, a tripod, a darkroom and chemical knowledge, and was the province of professionals and dedicated amateurs. Rolled film (first paper-backed, and from 1889 on a transparent celluloid base) removed nearly all of that. In 1900 the Brownie brought the price down to a dollar and put a camera within reach of children.

Ordinary people began to make a photographic record of their own lives, and the volume of images grew by orders of magnitude. The same flexible film stock was what made motion pictures possible, and press photography and the photographic documentation of war and politics followed from cameras that could be carried and used quickly.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kodak).

name: Guglielmo Marconi and wireless telegraphy
summary: Marconi transmitted radio signals without wires, solving the problem of communication to moving ships and remote locations.
body:
Guglielmo Marconi made radio a practical means of communication. Working from 1895 on his family's estate near Bologna, he combined a spark transmitter, a coherer receiver and, the addition that mattered most, a raised aerial and an earth connection, which extended the range of Hertz's laboratory demonstrations from metres to kilometres.

Marconi moved to Britain in 1896, patented the system there, and built it into a business selling both equipment and a service. He transmitted across the Bristol Channel in 1897, across the English Channel in 1899, and on 12 December 1901 reported receiving a signal sent from Cornwall at Signal Hill in Newfoundland, a claim disputed at the time, since the physics of long-distance propagation by reflection from the ionosphere was not yet known. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Karl Ferdinand Braun.

Wireless first proved itself at sea, where no cable can reach: the distress calls sent from the [Titanic](event:titanic-sinks) in 1912 brought the *Carpathia* to the lifeboats, and the disaster led to international rules requiring a continuous radio watch. Spark gave way to continuous-wave transmission and valve amplification, and by the 1920s the same technology had become broadcasting.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guglielmo_Marconi).

name: Discovery of X-rays
summary: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 while working with a cathode-ray tube; the first medical radiographs followed within weeks.
body:
On 8 November 1895, at Würzburg, Wilhelm Röntgen noticed that a screen coated with a fluorescent salt glowed while a covered cathode-ray tube was running nearby. Something was passing through the cardboard. He called it X-radiation, for the unknown, and within weeks had made the first radiograph of a human hand.

Röntgen established the essential properties in a few weeks of concentrated work: the rays travelled in straight lines, were not deflected by magnets, and were absorbed in proportion to the density and thickness of the material they passed through, so that bone stands out against flesh. He published in December 1895 and the news spread through the newspapers within days.

The medical use was immediate and obvious, and X-ray machines were in hospitals within a year, long before the dangers of the dose were understood; many early operators developed burns and cancers. In physics it set others hunting for similar emissions, which led Becquerel to [radioactivity](event:radioactivity) the following year, and X-ray diffraction later became the standard way of determining the arrangement of atoms in crystals, the method behind the [structure of DNA](event:dna-structure). Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray).

name: Cuban War of Independence
summary: Cuban insurgents fought Spanish rule for three years before American intervention in 1898 ended Spain's empire in the Americas and left the United States dominant on the island.
body:
The Cuban War of Independence began in February 1895 and was the last of three risings against Spanish rule on the island. After three years of guerrilla war the United States intervened, and the ten-week Spanish-American War that followed ended Spain's empire in the Americas and left the United States the dominant power in Cuba.

The rising was organised by José Martí, who was killed in its first weeks, and led in the field by Máximo Gómez and Antonio Maceo. Spain's response was to concentrate the rural population into garrison towns to separate it from the insurgents; hundreds of thousands died of hunger and disease in the *reconcentración*, and reporting of it in the American press built support for intervention. The explosion that destroyed the USS *Maine* in Havana harbour in February 1898 supplied the occasion.

Spain surrendered Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines by the Treaty of Paris in December 1898. Cuba was occupied by American forces until 1902 and became formally independent under the Platt Amendment, which gave the United States the right to intervene and a naval station at Guantánamo. American capital came to dominate the sugar economy, and the relationship this produced was still the central fact of Cuban politics when [Castro took power](event:castro-cuba) in 1959.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_War_of_Independence).

name: Discovery of radioactivity
summary: Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts emit radiation of their own accord, and Marie and Pierre Curie went on to isolate new radioactive elements.
body:
In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts fogged a photographic plate wrapped in black paper, without being heated or exposed to light first. The energy was coming from the uranium itself. This was radioactivity, and it was the first evidence that atoms are not permanent and indivisible.

Becquerel was following up the discovery of [X-rays](event:x-rays) and expected uranium's phosphorescence to be the cause; a run of cloudy weather in Paris left the plates in a drawer with the salt and produced the image anyway. [Marie and Pierre Curie](item:marie-curie) took up the phenomenon, measured it in every substance they could obtain, showed that its strength depended only on the quantity of the element present, and isolated polonium and radium from pitchblende in 1898. Ernest Rutherford then separated alpha and beta radiation and, with Frederick Soddy, showed that radioactive decay transmutes one element into another.

Radioactivity opened the interior of the atom to investigation and led directly to the nuclear model, to [nuclear fission](event:nuclear-fission) and to the [atomic bomb](event:trinity). It also gave geology a clock: the decay rates of long-lived isotopes are what date rocks, fossils and the age of the earth itself.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay).

name: Boxer Rebellion
summary: Chinese militia rose against foreign influence and Christian missionaries, besieging foreign legations in Beijing and prompting an international military response.
body:
Part of the [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). The Boxer Rebellion was an anti-foreign uprising in northern China between 1899 and 1901. Its members, from a movement the Chinese called the Righteous and Harmonious Fists, attacked missionaries, Chinese Christians, railways and telegraph lines, and in June 1900 besieged the foreign legation quarter in Beijing. An alliance of eight foreign powers broke the siege and occupied the capital.

The movement grew in Shandong out of drought, famine and resentment of foreign privileges won after the [Opium Wars](event:opium-wars). The Qing court, under the Empress Dowager Cixi, first tried to suppress it and then chose to back it, declaring war on the powers. Tens of thousands of Chinese Christians and many hundreds of foreign missionaries were killed.

The relief expedition, with Japanese, Russian, British, French, American, German, Italian and Austro-Hungarian contingents, reached Beijing on 14 August 1900. The occupying troops looted the city and mounted punitive expeditions in the countryside. The Boxer Protocol of 1901 imposed an indemnity of 450 million taels, payable over thirty-nine years, together with the execution of officials and the stationing of foreign troops on the route to the sea.

The indemnity strained Qing finances and the defeat further weakened the dynasty's standing, contributing to the [revolution of 1911](event:chinese-revolution).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxer_Rebellion).

name: Second Boer War
summary: British and colonial forces defeated the Afrikaner republics of South Africa and annexed them to the Empire.
body:
Part of the [Scramble for Africa](event:scramble-africa). The Second Boer War was fought from October 1899 to May 1902 between the British Empire and the two Afrikaner republics of South Africa, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. Britain won and annexed both, but the war took nearly three years and roughly 450,000 imperial troops to finish.

It began with Boer offensives that besieged Ladysmith, Kimberley and Mafeking, and a series of British defeats in December 1899. Massive reinforcement relieved the sieges and took the capitals by mid-1900, at which point the Boers dispersed into commandos and fought a guerrilla war for two more years. Britain answered with blockhouse lines, sweeps, farm burning, and the internment of the civilian population in camps. About 28,000 Boer internees died there, most of them children, and at least 20,000 black Africans died in separate camps; the reporting of the conditions by Emily Hobhouse caused a political crisis in Britain.

The Treaty of Vereeniging ended the war on British terms but promised self-government, which came in 1906–07, and left the franchise question in the conquered territories to be settled by their white electorates. That decision shaped the racial order of the Union of South Africa and later [apartheid](event:apartheid-end).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Boer_War).

name: First powered flight
summary: The Wright brothers flew a heavier-than-air powered machine under control at Kitty Hawk.
body:
On 17 December 1903, at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained, controlled flights of a powered heavier-than-air aircraft. The first covered 37 metres in 12 seconds; the fourth, with Wilbur flying, covered 260 metres in 59 seconds.

Others had built powered machines that left the ground. What the Wrights solved was control. From 1899 they worked through gliders and their own wind-tunnel measurements to a system of three-axis control (wing-warping for roll, a movable rudder for yaw and a forward elevator for pitch), and then built a light petrol engine and efficient propellers to match. Every aeroplane since has used the same three axes of control.

The brothers kept their work quiet while they sought patents and contracts, and public demonstrations in France and at Fort Myer in 1908 finally convinced sceptics. Military interest followed almost immediately, and aircraft were flying reconnaissance over the front by 1914.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_Flyer).

name: Suffragette movement in Britain
summary: British women, denied the vote, escalated from petitions to property damage and hunger strikes, forcing the question of female enfranchisement onto the political agenda.
body:
The suffragettes were members of the Women's Social and Political Union, founded by Emmeline Pankhurst in Manchester in 1903 to campaign for votes for women in Britain. Frustrated by decades of petitioning and lobbying that had produced nothing, they adopted the motto "Deeds not words" and escalated from heckling and demonstrations to window-breaking, arson and attacks on property.

The state responded with imprisonment; the prisoners responded with hunger strikes; the prisons responded with force-feeding, and then with the Act of 1913 that allowed the release and re-arrest of weakened prisoners. Emily Davison was killed stepping in front of the king's horse at the Derby that year. The campaign was widely reported and made the question impossible to set aside, though the far larger constitutional movement led by Millicent Fawcett argued that militancy was setting the cause back.

The WSPU suspended its campaign when [war](event:ww1) began in 1914. The Representation of the People Act of 1918 gave the vote to women over thirty who met a property qualification, and the Equal Franchise Act of 1928 extended it on the same terms as men. [Finland](event:finland-suffrage), New Zealand and Australia had all done so earlier.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffragette).

name: Russo-Japanese War
summary: Japan and Russia fought for control of Korea and Manchuria; Japan won, the first modern victory of an Asian state over a European great power.
body:
The Russo-Japanese War was fought in 1904 and 1905 over rival ambitions in Manchuria and Korea. Japan won it, and became the first Asian state in the modern era to defeat a European great power in a full-scale war.

Japan opened with a surprise attack on the Russian squadron at Port Arthur in February 1904 and landed armies in Korea and on the Liaodong peninsula. The fighting on land was heavy, entrenched and fed by rail; the siege of Port Arthur and the battle of Mukden in early 1905, where about half a million men were engaged, both anticipated the Western Front. The decisive blow was at sea: the Baltic Fleet sailed 33,000 kilometres to reach the theatre and was annihilated at Tsushima in May 1905 in a single afternoon.

Neither state could afford to continue. The Treaty of Portsmouth, mediated by Theodore Roosevelt, gave Japan the Liaodong lease, the southern half of Sakhalin and a free hand in Korea, which it annexed in 1910. Defeat cost the Russian government its remaining authority and set off the revolution of 1905, and the result was noted across Asia, in China, India and the Ottoman Empire, as evidence that a European power could be defeated.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Japanese_War).

name: Einstein's theory of relativity
summary: Einstein's relativity described space and time as aspects of a single flexible geometry, and mass as a form of energy.
body:
Between 1905 and 1915 [Albert Einstein](item:albert-einstein) published the two theories of relativity. Special relativity made the speed of light the same for every observer and abandoned absolute time; general relativity replaced the force of gravity with the curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy. Together they are the framework in which large-scale physics is done.

Special relativity resolved a contradiction between Newtonian mechanics, in which velocities simply add, and Maxwell's electromagnetism, which gives light a fixed speed. Einstein's resolution was to keep the fixed speed and give up simultaneity: moving clocks run slow, moving lengths contract, and mass and energy are the same quantity in different units. General relativity, ten years later, explained the anomalous precession of Mercury's orbit and predicted that starlight passing the sun would be deflected, which was measured during the eclipse of 1919 and made Einstein famous outside physics.

The effects are not confined to extreme conditions. Satellite navigation must correct for both the speed of its clocks and the weaker gravity at orbital height. Black holes, the expanding universe and [gravitational waves](event:gravitational-waves) all follow from general relativity, and the last of these was detected a century after it was written down. See the article on [relativity](item:theory-of-relativity) for the theory itself.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_relativity).

name: Relativity
summary: The theory that space and time form a single flexible geometry, that the speed of light is the same for every observer, and that gravity is the curvature of that geometry.
body:
Relativity is the theory that space and time form a single flexible geometry, that light travels at the same speed for every observer, and that gravity is the curvature of that geometry rather than a force acting across it. It is the framework for physics at large scales, from satellite navigation to cosmology.

Special relativity, published by [Einstein](item:albert-einstein) in 1905, begins from two propositions: the laws of physics are the same for all observers in uniform motion, and light travels at the same speed for all of them. Absolute simultaneity, absolute length and absolute time do not survive. Moving clocks run slow, moving lengths contract, and mass and energy turn out to be the same quantity in different units.

General relativity followed in 1915. Gravity is not a force acting across space but the curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy; bodies in free fall follow the straightest available paths through it. The theory predicted the precession of Mercury's orbit, the bending of starlight confirmed in 1919, and the slowing of clocks in a gravitational field that satellite navigation must correct for.

Its stranger predictions took a century to confirm: black holes, the expansion of the universe, and [gravitational waves](item:gravitational-waves), first detected in 2015. Relativity has so far agreed with every experiment and has not been reconciled with quantum mechanics. See also the entry on [Einstein's theory of relativity](item:relativity).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_relativity).

name: Finland grants women's suffrage
summary: Finland became the first European nation to grant women full voting and candidacy rights.
body:
In 1906 the Grand Duchy of Finland, then an autonomous part of the Russian Empire, replaced its four-estate diet with a single-chamber parliament elected by universal suffrage. Finland became the first country in the world to grant women both the vote and the right to stand for election, and the first in Europe to give women the parliamentary vote at all.

Women had voted before this (in the Wyoming Territory from 1869, in New Zealand from 1893, and in South Australia, where they could also stand, from 1894), but Finland was the first sovereign-level parliament to combine both rights without qualification. The reform came out of the general strike of 1905, during which Russian authority in Finland briefly collapsed, and out of a national movement in which women's organisations had been prominent for decades.

The first election was held in March 1907 and returned nineteen women to a parliament of two hundred, the first women members of a national legislature anywhere. Russia dissolved the parliament repeatedly in the years that followed, and it acquired real power only with Finnish independence in 1917. The other Nordic countries enfranchised women between 1913 and 1921, Britain and the United States by 1928, and much of the rest of the world after [1945](event:ww2).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage_in_Finland).

name: Bosnian Crisis
summary: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, triggering a crisis with Russia and Serbia that brought Europe close to war six years before [1914](event:ww1).
body:
In October 1908 Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina, which it had occupied and administered since 1878 while the territory remained formally Ottoman. The annexation broke the Treaty of Berlin, enraged Serbia, and produced a six-month diplomatic crisis that brought the European powers close to war.

The move was timed to the Young Turk revolution, which threatened to draw the province back into a reforming Ottoman state. Serbia wanted Bosnia for itself and mobilised; Russia claimed to speak for Slavic interests but had not recovered from defeat by [Japan](event:russo-japanese-war) and had been outmanoeuvred by its own foreign minister's private understanding with Vienna. Germany then backed Austria unconditionally and demanded that Russia recognise the annexation and press Serbia to do the same. In March 1909 Russia gave way.

The settlement resolved little. Russia treated the outcome as a defeat to be reversed and accelerated its rearmament; Serbian ambitions hardened, and secret societies took up what the government could not do openly; Germany had backed Austria-Hungary unconditionally and did so again in 1914. The same alignments produced the crisis of July that year, after the [assassination at Sarajevo](event:sarajevo).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_crisis_of_1908%E2%80%9309).

name: Blériot's Channel crossing
summary: Louis Blériot flew a monoplane across the English Channel, proving that aircraft could make practical journeys and making invasion by air conceivable.
body:
On 25 July 1909 Louis Blériot flew a monoplane of his own design from near Calais to Dover, crossing the English Channel in about 37 minutes. He won the £1,000 prize offered by the *Daily Mail*, and made the first flight across a significant body of water in a heavier-than-air machine.

Blériot had spent his fortune on a series of failed designs before the Blériot XI, a wire-braced monoplane with a three-cylinder engine of 25 horsepower. He flew without a compass, lost sight of land in the middle of the crossing, and landed heavily in a meadow behind Dover Castle. Hubert Latham had ditched in the sea attempting the same crossing six days earlier.

The flight had an effect out of proportion to its length because of what it implied. The [Wrights](event:wright-flyer) had shown that flight was possible; Blériot showed that an aircraft could be taken from one country to another on a chosen day. British commentary turned at once to the fact that the Channel was no longer a moat, and orders for Blériot's aircraft followed from several governments. Within five years aeroplanes were flying reconnaissance over the front in [France](event:ww1).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Bl%C3%A9riot).

name: Scott's Antarctic Expedition
summary: Robert Falcon Scott led an expedition to the South Pole, reaching it only to find he had been beaten by Amundsen; he and his party died on the return.
body:
The Terra Nova expedition of 1910–13, led by Robert Falcon Scott, was a British scientific and exploring expedition to Antarctica whose polar party reached the South Pole on 17 January 1912 and found that Roald Amundsen had been there thirty-four days earlier. All five men died on the return march.

The expedition landed 65 men at Cape Evans on Ross Island and ran a scientific programme in geology, meteorology, glaciology and zoology that brought back over 2,000 specimens, among them fossil plants from the Beardmore Glacier that were later evidence for continental drift. A winter journey to collect emperor penguin eggs at Cape Crozier became famous on its own account.

The march to the Pole used a mixture of motor sledges, ponies and dogs in the early stages and man-hauling for the last and longest, a method that demanded more calories than the ration provided. On the way back Edgar Evans died in February and Lawrence Oates, crippled by frostbite, walked out of the tent into a blizzard in March. Scott, Edward Wilson and Henry Bowers were pinned by a blizzard and died at the end of March, eleven miles short of the supply depot called One Ton.

A search party found the tent, the bodies, the diaries and 16 kilograms of geological specimens the men had dragged to the end. Scott's last letters made him a national figure, and the argument over whether the disaster was bad luck or bad planning has continued ever since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Nova_Expedition).

name: Xinhai Revolution ends the Qing dynasty
summary: The Xinhai Revolution ended more than two and a half centuries of Qing rule and over two thousand years of imperial government, installing a republic that soon fractured under warlords.
body:
Part of the [Qing dynasty](event:qing-dynasty). The Xinhai Revolution overthrew the Qing dynasty and ended more than two thousand years of imperial government in China. It began with a mutiny at Wuchang on 10 October 1911 and ended with the abdication of the six-year-old emperor Puyi on 12 February 1912, in favour of a republic.

The dynasty had been discredited by defeat in the [Opium Wars](event:opium-wars), by the indemnity imposed after the [Boxer Rebellion](event:boxer-rebellion), and by reforms that came too late and too grudgingly. The immediate trigger was a plan to nationalise the provincial railways with foreign loans, which turned the propertied classes of Sichuan against Beijing, and an accidental bomb explosion in Hankou that exposed a revolutionary cell inside the army and forced its hand.

Province after province declared independence from the court over the following weeks. Sun Yat-sen, whose Tongmenghui had organised repeated failed risings, returned from abroad and was made provisional president of a republic at Nanjing; he handed the office to Yuan Shikai, the general who commanded the only modern army, in exchange for the emperor's abdication.

The republic did not hold. Yuan dissolved parliament and declared himself emperor in 1915, and after his death in 1916 the country broke into more than a decade of warlord rule, followed by [Japanese invasion](event:sino-japanese-war) and civil war.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinhai_Revolution).

name: RMS Titanic sinks
summary: The largest ship in the world struck an iceberg on her maiden voyage and sank, killing about 1,500 people.
body:
RMS *Titanic*, the largest ship afloat and four days out from Southampton on her maiden voyage to New York, struck an iceberg late on 14 April 1912 and sank in the North Atlantic in the early hours of the 15th. About 1,500 of the roughly 2,220 people aboard died.

The ship's hull was divided into sixteen watertight compartments and she could float with any four of them flooded. The iceberg opened at least five. She sank in two hours and forty minutes in water at about −2 °C, in which nobody unprotected survives for long.

There were lifeboats for 1,178 people, more than the regulations of the time required and barely half of those on board, and several were launched partly filled. Survival tracked class and sex: almost all the women in first class were saved, and the majority of third-class passengers, held below by the ship's layout and by delay, were not. The *Carpathia*, called by wireless, reached the boats about four hours after the sinking.

The inquiries that followed produced the first International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea in 1914: lifeboat places for everyone aboard, boat drills, a continuous radio watch, and an ice patrol in the North Atlantic that still operates.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_Titanic).

name: Alan Turing
summary: English mathematician who defined what a computation is, broke German naval ciphers during the Second World War, and framed the question of machine intelligence.
body:
Turing's 1936 paper on computable numbers answered a problem in mathematical logic by imagining an abstract machine reading and writing symbols on a tape. The Turing machine settled which questions no procedure can decide, and defined the notion of an algorithm that every later computer implements.

At Bletchley Park during [the Second World War](item:ww2) he designed the bombe, an electromechanical machine that searched Enigma settings, and led the section that broke the naval ciphers directing the U-boat campaign in the Atlantic. The work stayed secret for decades; historians generally credit Bletchley's output with shortening the war.

Afterwards he designed one of the first stored-program computers, wrote on the chemical basis of pattern formation in biology, and in 1950 proposed the imitation game, a test of whether a machine's replies can be told from a person's, as a way of replacing the unanswerable question of whether machines think; among the objections he answered there was [Lovelace's](item:ada-lovelace), that a machine can originate nothing. In 1952 he was prosecuted for homosexuality and accepted hormone treatment in place of prison; he died two years later of cyanide poisoning, ruled a suicide. The British government apologised in 2009 and pardoned him in 2013.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing).

name: Ford assembly line
summary: Henry Ford introduced the moving assembly line to automobile manufacturing, allowing mass production and making cars affordable for ordinary workers.
body:
The Ford Motor Company put a moving assembly line into operation at its Highland Park plant near Detroit in 1913. Chassis were pulled past workers who each performed one operation, instead of being built in place by teams that moved around them. The time to assemble a Model T fell from over twelve hours to about ninety minutes.

The idea was assembled from existing practice (the disassembly lines of Chicago meatpacking, interchangeable parts, and conveyors from grain milling and brewing) and applied to a single unchanging product. The saving went into the price: a Model T cost $850 in 1908 and under $300 by the mid-1920s, and roughly half the cars in the world were Model Ts. In 1914 Ford doubled wages to five dollars a day, partly to stop the turnover that the monotony of the line was causing.

Mass production spread far beyond cars, to appliances, aircraft and Soviet tractor plants, and "Fordism" became a name for an entire industrial model of standardised goods, high wages and mass consumption. Its costs were the deskilling of the work and the pace set by the belt rather than by the worker.

Cheap cars changed patterns of settlement, making suburbs and commuting common.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_line).

name: Panama Canal opens
summary: A canal of locks and an artificial lake joined the Atlantic and Pacific, cutting some 13,000 kilometres from the voyage between New York and San Francisco.
body:
The Panama Canal opened to traffic on 15 August 1914, when the cargo ship *Ancon* made the first official transit. Its 82 kilometres of channel, locks and artificial lake join the Atlantic to the Pacific and remove some 13,000 kilometres from the voyage between New York and San Francisco.

A French company under Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had built [Suez](event:suez-canal), attempted a sea-level cut from 1881 and failed: the rock of the Culebra Cut slid back into the excavation, and yellow fever and malaria killed something over 20,000 workers. The United States took the project over in 1904, after backing Panama's separation from Colombia and obtaining rights over a canal zone.

The American engineers changed the design to a system of locks fed by a dammed lake, and began with a sanitary campaign: William Gorgas, acting on the newly established role of the mosquito, drained, oiled and screened the towns and effectively ended yellow fever on the isthmus. Malaria and accidents still killed about 5,600 workers, most of them West Indian labourers.

The canal let the United States move a fleet between two oceans and confirmed its dominance in the Caribbean. Washington governed the Canal Zone as its own territory until 1979 and handed the waterway to Panama at the end of 1999.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_Canal).

name: Assassination of Franz Ferdinand
summary: Gavrilo Princip shot the Austrian heir in Sarajevo, setting off the July Crisis.
body:
Part of [World War I](event:ww1). Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie were shot dead in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb. The killing set off the July Crisis and, five weeks later, the [First World War](event:ww1).

Bosnia had been [annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908](event:bosnian-crisis), and Princip belonged to Young Bosnia, a group of students who wanted the South Slav provinces joined to Serbia. Six assassins were placed along the route of the Archduke's motorcade, armed and trained with the help of officers of the Serbian military intelligence service. A bomb thrown earlier in the morning missed. The car took a wrong turning on the way back from the town hall and stopped to reverse a few metres from where Princip was standing.

Vienna held the Serbian government responsible and, with German backing, sent an ultimatum designed to be rejected. Serbia accepted almost all of it; Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July. Princip was too young to be executed under Habsburg law and died of tuberculosis in prison in 1918.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Archduke_Franz_Ferdinand).

name: World War I
summary: Four years of industrial-scale war killed some 20 million people and destroyed four empires.
body:
World War I was fought from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918 between the Allies (chiefly France, Russia, Britain and their empires, with Italy from 1915 and the United States from 1917) and the Central Powers of Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria. Estimates of the dead run from 15 to 22 million, soldiers and civilians together. The Central Powers were defeated, and four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman) did not survive the war.

The immediate cause was the [assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand](event:sarajevo) in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, which Austria-Hungary used to force a reckoning with Serbia. Behind it stood a system of alliances, a naval and military arms race, and a Balkan question the powers had already brought themselves to the edge over in [1908](event:bosnian-crisis). Within five weeks of the murder, mobilisation timetables and treaty obligations had drawn in every great power in Europe.

Germany's opening plan was to knock France out quickly by marching through Belgium and then turn east. It failed at the Marne, and by the end of 1914 the Western Front was a continuous line of trenches from the Channel to the Swiss border. Artillery, machine guns, barbed wire and railways gave the defender an advantage that neither side could break for three years; the offensives mounted to break it (Verdun, the Somme, Passchendaele) cost hundreds of thousands of casualties for a few kilometres. The war was fought as well in Russia and Galicia, in the Alps, at Gallipoli, in Mesopotamia and Palestine, in Africa, and at sea, where the British blockade and the German submarine campaign attacked each other's food and trade.

It was also the first war fought by whole societies: conscription, war economies, rationing, censorship and propaganda, and women in factories and offices in numbers there had been no precedent for. The strain broke Russia first, in [revolution](event:russian-revolution) in 1917, and Germany last, in mutiny and revolution in the autumn of 1918.

The armistice of 11 November 1918 was followed by the [Treaty of Versailles](event:versailles) and the settlements with the other defeated states. They redrew central Europe into new national states, distributed the Ottoman provinces of the Middle East as mandates, and imposed reparations and war guilt on Germany. The peace left grievances that were still live twenty years later, and the mobilised armies helped carry the [influenza pandemic](event:spanish-flu) around the world as they went home.

The steps below follow the war from the July Crisis to the armistice.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I).

steps.name: The July Crisis
steps.page:
The heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne was [shot at Sarajevo](item:sarajevo) on 28 June 1914. Vienna held Serbia responsible, obtained Germany's promise of support, and on 23 July sent an ultimatum written to be refused; Serbia accepted almost all of it, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July.

Russia mobilised in Serbia's support. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and invaded Belgium on 4 August to turn the French frontier defences; Britain, a guarantor of Belgian neutrality, declared war the same evening. Five of Europe's six great powers were at war within a week.

steps.name: The Marne
steps.page:
The German advance came within about 50 km of Paris before a gap opened between its two right-flank armies. French and British forces counter-attacked into it between 5 and 12 September 1914 and forced a German withdrawal to the Aisne.

The battle ended any prospect of a short war in the west. Both sides then extended their lines northwards to the sea, and by November the front was a continuous entrenched line from Nieuwpoort to the Swiss frontier that moved very little for the next three years.

steps.name: Gallipoli
steps.page:
An Anglo-French naval attempt to force the Dardanelles failed in March 1915, and troops were landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April to take the straits from the land. Ottoman forces held the high ground above the beaches, and the campaign settled into trench fighting as static as the Western Front.

The Allies evacuated in December 1915 and January 1916 without having advanced beyond their landing areas. Around half a million casualties were suffered on the two sides; the campaign is a founding memory in Australia, New Zealand and Turkey alike.

steps.name: The United States enters
steps.page:
Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, accepting American belligerency as the price of starving Britain out before it took effect. The Zimmermann telegram, in which Berlin offered Mexico an alliance and the recovery of its lost territories, was intercepted and published in March.

Congress declared war on 6 April 1917. American troops arrived slowly, about 175,000 by the end of the year but over a million by mid-1918, and the certainty of their arrival shaped both sides' plans for the following year.

steps.name: Russia leaves the war
steps.page:
The [Bolsheviks](item:october-revolution) took power in November 1917 committed to ending the war, and signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918. Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic provinces, Finland and Ukraine, a third of its population and much of its industry and grain.

The treaty freed some fifty German divisions for the Western Front and was annulled by the armistice in the west eight months later.

steps.name: The German spring offensive
steps.page:
Germany attacked on 21 March 1918 with divisions brought from the east, using short hurricane bombardments and infantry trained to infiltrate rather than to advance in line. The British Fifth Army was driven back some 60 km in a week, the deepest advance in the west since 1914, and further offensives followed in Flanders and on the Aisne.

The attacks took ground but not the railway junctions they needed, and cost about a million casualties the German army could not replace. The last of them was stopped on the Marne in July.

steps.name: The Hundred Days and the armistice
steps.page:
The Allied counter-offensive opened at Amiens on 8 August 1918 with tanks, aircraft and predicted artillery fire, and did not stop. Through the autumn the German army was pushed back off the Hindenburg Line while Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary left the war in turn.

Mutiny in the German fleet at Kiel spread into revolution; the Kaiser abdicated on 9 November. The armistice was signed in a railway carriage at Compiègne and took effect at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918.

name: Easter Rising in Dublin
summary: Irish republicans seized buildings in central Dublin and proclaimed a republic; the rising was put down within a week, and the executions that followed turned Irish opinion towards the republicans.
body:
About 1,200 Irish republicans seized the General Post Office and other buildings in central Dublin on Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, and proclaimed an Irish Republic. The British army brought in artillery and a gunboat; the rebels surrendered after six days, with much of the city centre in ruins and some 485 people dead, most of them civilians.

The rising was organised by the Irish Republican Brotherhood inside the Irish Volunteers, with James Connolly's Irish Citizen Army, and timed to the [war](event:ww1) in the belief that England's difficulty was Ireland's opportunity. A German arms shipment was intercepted and the Volunteers' own commander countermanded the mobilisation, so the turnout was a fraction of what had been planned and confined largely to Dublin.

Dubliners were at first hostile to the rebels. What changed opinion was the aftermath: fifteen leaders were shot by firing squad at Kilmainham over ten days, Connolly tied to a chair because he could not stand, and thousands were interned without trial.

Sinn Féin, wrongly blamed for the rising at the time, won 73 of Ireland's 105 seats in the general election of December 1918 and set up its own parliament rather than sit at Westminster. The [war of independence](event:irish-independence) followed in 1919.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Rising).

name: Battle of Verdun
summary: Ten months of attrition around a French fortress city cost some 700,000 casualties.
body:
Part of [World War I](event:ww1). The Battle of Verdun was fought from 21 February to 18 December 1916 around the fortified city of Verdun on the Meuse. It was the longest battle of the [First World War](event:ww1), and the two armies together suffered something like 700,000 casualties, of whom about 300,000 were killed.

The German commander, Erich von Falkenhayn, chose a sector the French would defend for reasons of prestige, intending to bleed their army white rather than to break through. The attack opened with a bombardment of about a million shells on a narrow front and took Fort Douaumont, the strongest work of the ring, within four days.

The French put Philippe Pétain in command, held, and rotated most of the divisions of their army through the sector so that the burden was shared and most French soldiers passed through the sector. Supplies came up a single road, the *Voie Sacrée*, by lorry convoy running day and night. The German advance was halted in July, when the [Somme](event:somme) offensive drew off their reserves, and French counter-attacks recovered Douaumont in October and most of the lost ground by December.

The battle ended roughly where it had begun. It became the central French memory of the war, and the phrase *ils ne passeront pas* ("they shall not pass") is associated with it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Verdun).

name: Battle of the Somme
summary: Nearly 60,000 British casualties fell on the first day; tanks appeared in battle for the first time.
body:
Part of [World War I](event:ww1). The Battle of the Somme was fought from 1 July to 18 November 1916 on both banks of the river Somme in Picardy. It was the largest battle of the [First World War](event:ww1) on the Western Front, and cost over a million casualties on the two sides.

It was planned as a joint Franco-British offensive, but the German attack at [Verdun](event:verdun) in February took most of the French divisions intended for it, and the weight fell on Kitchener's new volunteer armies. A seven-day bombardment was expected to destroy the German wire and dugouts; much of it did not, and on 1 July the British army suffered 57,470 casualties, of them 19,240 killed, the worst day in its history.

The offensive continued for four and a half months as a series of limited attacks in worsening weather. Tanks were used in action for the first time on 15 September at Flers-Courcelette, in small numbers and with mixed results. When it was called off in November the Allies had advanced about ten kilometres.

Historians continue to disagree over whether the battle was a futile slaughter or a necessary attrition of the German field army, which German accounts afterwards described as having been buried on the Somme.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Somme).

name: Russian Revolution
summary: Tsarism fell and the Bolsheviks built the world's first communist state.
body:
The Russian Revolution was the collapse of the Russian monarchy in 1917 and the seizure of power by the Bolsheviks eight months later, followed by a civil war that they won. It produced the world's first state governed by a communist party, which in 1922 became the [Soviet Union](event:ussr-founded).

Three years of [war](event:ww1) had cost Russia millions of casualties and wrecked the supply of food and fuel to its cities. In March 1917 bread queues and strikes in Petrograd turned into a general revolt that the garrison refused to put down, and Nicholas II abdicated. Power was then shared uneasily between a Provisional Government of liberals and moderate socialists and the soviets (councils of workers' and soldiers' deputies), which held the loyalty of the armed crowd.

The Provisional Government's decision to stay in the war destroyed it. Lenin, returned from exile in April, offered peace, land and bread and put the Bolsheviks in permanent opposition to it; a failed military intervention in September left the government without support on either side. On 7 November the Bolsheviks took Petrograd almost without a fight.

The new government made peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk, dissolved the elected Constituent Assembly after a single day, nationalised industry and land, and met resistance with a political police. Civil war followed against White armies, nationalist governments and foreign expeditionary forces; it killed several million people, most of them by hunger and typhus rather than by fighting, and the Bolsheviks won it by 1922.

[Communist](event:communist-manifesto) parties elsewhere took the Bolshevik party as their model, and relations between the Soviet state and the Western powers became the [Cold War](event:cold-war) after 1945.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Revolution).

steps.name: The February Revolution
steps.page:
Strikes and bread riots in Petrograd on 8 March 1917 (International Women's Day, and 23 February in the old Russian calendar) grew within days into a general rising. The regiments of the city garrison sent to disperse the crowds mutinied and joined them.

The Duma formed a Provisional Government while the reconstituted Petrograd Soviet claimed the loyalty of the soldiers. Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March, and his brother refused the throne the next day; three centuries of Romanov rule ended in a week.

steps.name: Dual power
steps.page:
Through the spring and summer the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet governed against each other, the one with legal authority, the other with the garrison and the railways. Lenin returned from Switzerland in April demanding an immediate peace, land to the peasants and all power to the soviets.

The government chose instead to honour its commitments to the Allies and launched an offensive in June, which collapsed. Armed demonstrations in Petrograd in July (the July Days) were put down, Lenin fled to Finland, and Alexander Kerensky became prime minister.

steps.name: The Kornilov affair
steps.page:
In September 1917 the commander-in-chief, Lavr Kornilov, moved troops towards Petrograd. Whether he was acting with Kerensky's agreement against the left or against the government itself is still disputed; Kerensky dismissed him and appealed to the Soviet for defence.

Railwaymen stopped the trains and agitators talked the advancing units apart, and the affair ended in four days without fighting. It destroyed what credit the government had left with the officer corps, and the Bolsheviks, released from prison and armed to meet the threat, emerged from it with a majority in the Petrograd Soviet.

steps.name: The Civil War
steps.page:
The Bolsheviks held the centre (Petrograd, Moscow and the railways between them) against White armies in Siberia, the south and the north-west, nationalist governments in Ukraine, the Caucasus and the Baltic, peasant risings, and British, French, American and Japanese expeditionary forces.

Trotsky built the Red Army from conscripts and former tsarist officers; grain was requisitioned from the villages to feed the towns. Several million people died, the great majority of typhus, hunger and reprisal rather than in battle. The last White forces left Vladivostok in October 1922.

steps.name: Kronstadt and the New Economic Policy
steps.page:
In March 1921 the sailors of the Kronstadt naval base, who had been among the most reliable supporters of the revolution, rose against the government demanding free soviets and an end to grain requisitioning. The rising was crushed across the ice within a fortnight.

At the same congress the party abandoned the requisitioning that had provoked it. The New Economic Policy allowed private trade and small enterprise while the state kept heavy industry, banking and foreign trade, and the economy recovered from a famine that had killed some five million people.

name: October Revolution
summary: Bolshevik forces seized the Winter Palace and the organs of the Provisional Government in Petrograd.
body:
Part of [Russian Revolution](event:russian-revolution). On 7 November 1917 (25 October in the Russian calendar of the time, which is why it is called the October Revolution) Bolshevik forces took control of Petrograd and overthrew the Provisional Government. It brought Lenin's party to power in Russia.

The operation was run by the Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet under Leon Trotsky, using Red Guards, sailors from Kronstadt and units of the garrison. Bridges, telegraph offices, railway stations and power stations were occupied through the day against almost no resistance. The Winter Palace, defended by cadets and a women's battalion, was entered late in the evening after a blank shot from the cruiser *Aurora*, and the ministers inside were arrested after midnight. There were very few casualties.

The Second Congress of Soviets, meeting as this happened, approved the transfer of power; the Menshevik and Socialist-Revolutionary delegates walked out. The new government's first decrees offered an immediate peace and gave the landlords' estates to the peasants.

Elections to a Constituent Assembly held in November returned a Socialist-Revolutionary majority; the assembly met once, in January 1918, and was dispersed by armed guards. [Civil war](event:russian-revolution) followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/October_Revolution).

name: Nelson Mandela
summary: South African lawyer and revolutionary who spent twenty-seven years in prison and then negotiated the end of apartheid as the country's first democratically elected president.
body:
Mandela was born into the Thembu royal house in the Transkei, trained as a lawyer, and opened the first black law practice in Johannesburg with Oliver Tambo. As apartheid legislation hardened after 1948 he helped build the African National Congress Youth League and organised campaigns of defiance.

After the Sharpeville massacre and the banning of the ANC he abandoned strictly non-violent tactics and co-founded its armed wing, arguing that sabotage was the least destructive of the remaining options. He was convicted of sabotage at the Rivonia Trial in 1964 and sentenced to life, spending eighteen years on Robben Island; the speech he gave from the dock, ending with a cause for which he was prepared to die, became the movement's text.

International sanctions, internal revolt from the [Soweto uprising](item:soweto-uprising) onwards and a bankrupt policy brought the government to negotiate. Released in 1990, he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk, and in 1994 was elected president in [South Africa's first universal-suffrage election](item:apartheid-end). He served one term, preferring reconciliation and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to retribution, and stepped down.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela).

name: Spanish flu pandemic
summary: An H1N1 influenza pandemic infected perhaps a third of humanity and killed tens of millions.
body:
The influenza pandemic of 1918–1920 was caused by an H1N1 virus and is the deadliest pandemic of the twentieth century. It infected around 500 million people, about a third of the world's population, and estimates of the dead range from 17 million to over 100 million; 25 to 50 million is the figure usually quoted.

The virus was unusual in whom it killed. Ordinary influenza is most dangerous to infants and the old; this one killed healthy adults between about twenty and forty in very large numbers, probably by provoking an overwhelming immune response in the lungs.

The pandemic is called the Spanish flu because of wartime censorship. Spain was neutral in the [First World War](event:ww1) and reported its epidemic freely, while the warring states suppressed the news to protect morale, so the outbreak appeared to belong to Spain. The earliest documented cases were in Kansas in early 1918. Troop trains, crowded camps and the movement of armies carried it around the world in months.

There were no vaccines, no antivirals and no antibiotics for the pneumonia that killed most victims. The measures that worked were the ones available in 1918: isolation, quarantine, closing schools and public gatherings, and banning mass meetings. Cities that acted early and kept the restrictions in place had markedly lower death rates.

The pandemic came in waves, and they are set out in the steps below.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu).

steps.name: The first wave
steps.page:
The first recognised outbreak ran through the spring and early summer of 1918. It spread very fast in army camps and in the ports and railways feeding the [Western Front](item:ww1), but killed at close to ordinary influenza rates, and in several countries it was recorded as a mild three-day fever.

By the summer it had reached most of Europe, North America and India, and had died away in many places. It left behind an infected population on both sides of a war that was moving millions of men between continents.

steps.name: The second wave
steps.page:
The second wave began in August 1918 and was far deadlier, killing within days through a viral pneumonia that could turn a patient blue for lack of oxygen. October 1918 was the worst month of the pandemic almost everywhere it reached.

Hospitals and undertakers were overwhelmed; some cities banned public gatherings and closed schools, theatres and churches, and the places that did so early and for long enough recorded markedly lower mortality. Most of the deaths of the whole pandemic fell in these four months.

steps.name: The third wave
steps.page:
A third wave ran from January to the late spring of 1919, less lethal than the second but heavy in Britain, Spain, Serbia, Mexico and Australia, which its quarantine had held off until then.

It reached the Paris peace conference: Woodrow Wilson fell seriously ill with influenza in April 1919 in the middle of the negotiation of the [Treaty of Versailles](item:versailles).

steps.name: The fourth wave
steps.page:
A final wave through the winter of 1919–20 struck parts of Europe, the United States and Japan. It was milder again, and by the spring of 1920 the pandemic had faded as the surviving population's immunity spread.

Descendants of the 1918 virus circulate still: every seasonal H1N1 influenza since, and the pandemics of 1957, 1968 and 2009, derive from it.

name: Treaty of Versailles
summary: The peace imposed on Germany assigned it war guilt and reparations, and redrew the map of Europe.
body:
Part of [World War I](event:ww1). The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, five years to the day after the [assassination at Sarajevo](event:sarajevo), and ended the state of war between Germany and the Allied powers. Germany was not a party to the negotiations and signed under threat of invasion.

The terms were drawn up in Paris chiefly by Britain, France and the United States. Germany lost about 13 per cent of its territory and all its colonies: Alsace-Lorraine to France, most of Posen and West Prussia to a restored Poland, the Saar coalfield to French administration for fifteen years. Its army was capped at 100,000 men with no tanks, submarines or air force, and the Rhineland was demilitarised and occupied. Article 231 assigned responsibility for the war and its damage to Germany and its allies, and was the legal basis for reparations later fixed at 132 billion gold marks.

The treaty also created the League of Nations, whose covenant formed its first part. The United States Senate refused to ratify either, and the United States never joined the League.

In Germany the settlement was called the *Diktat* and rejected across the political spectrum, a grievance the Nazi party built on. Separate treaties (Saint-Germain, Trianon, Neuilly and Sèvres) dealt with Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles).

name: American Prohibition
summary: The United States banned the manufacture, sale and transport of alcohol from 1920 to 1933; the trade passed to criminal suppliers and the ban was repealed.
body:
Prohibition in the United States was the national ban on the manufacture, sale and transport of alcoholic drink, in force from January 1920 to December 1933 under the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act that enforced it.

It was the achievement of a temperance movement a century old, backed by Protestant churches, progressive reformers and the Anti-Saloon League, and directed at the saloon as much as at drink itself. Consumption did fall, particularly at first, and deaths from cirrhosis and drunkenness declined.

What it also did was hand a large consumer market to criminal suppliers. Smuggling from Canada and the Caribbean, industrial alcohol diverted and redistilled (sometimes lethally), and speakeasies in every city supported organised crime on a new scale, of which Al Capone's Chicago operation was the best known. Enforcement was underfunded and widely corrupted, and the law was openly flouted.

The Depression made the case against it economic as well: legal drink meant tax revenue and jobs. Repeal was a plank of Franklin Roosevelt's 1932 campaign, and the Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth in December 1933. It is the only amendment to the United States Constitution to have been repealed, and the only one ratified by state conventions rather than legislatures. Several states stayed dry for years afterwards.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition_in_the_United_States).

name: Irish independence
summary: After a two-year war of independence, the Anglo-Irish Treaty created the Irish Free State as a dominion and partitioned the island.
body:
The Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed on 6 December 1921 and created the Irish Free State, a self-governing dominion of the British Empire covering twenty-six of Ireland's thirty-two counties. It ended the War of Independence fought since January 1919 between the Irish Republican Army and British forces.

The war grew out of the [Easter Rising](event:easter-rising) and the election of December 1918, in which Sinn Féin won most Irish seats and set up its own parliament, the Dáil, rather than sit at Westminster. It was fought as ambush and reprisal: flying columns against police barracks, and the Black and Tans and Auxiliaries burning towns and shooting suspects. Around 2,000 people were killed.

The treaty gave Ireland fiscal and military independence but required an oath to the Crown, left three naval ports in British hands, and confirmed the partition already made in 1920, with six northern counties remaining in the United Kingdom. Éamon de Valera and a large minority of the Dáil rejected it, and the split produced a civil war in 1922–23 that killed more Irish people than the war against Britain had.

The Free State removed the last constitutional links with Britain over the following decades and declared itself a republic in 1949. Partition remained, and with it the conflict in Northern Ireland.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_War_of_Independence).

name: Discovery of insulin
summary: Frederick Banting and Charles Best extracted insulin from the pancreas, providing the first effective treatment for diabetes and saving millions of lives.
body:
Insulin was isolated at the University of Toronto in 1921 and used to treat a diabetic patient for the first time in January 1922. It turned type 1 diabetes from a disease that killed children within months into one that can be managed for a lifetime.

Frederick Banting, a surgeon, and Charles Best, a student assistant, working in J. J. R. Macleod's laboratory, tied off the pancreatic ducts of dogs to let the digestive tissue waste away and then extracted the surviving islet tissue. The extract lowered blood sugar in diabetic dogs. James Collip then purified it enough to be injected into people.

The first patient, Leonard Thompson, was fourteen and close to death; he recovered and lived another thirteen years. Eli Lilly began industrial production within a year, and insulin extracted from pig and cattle pancreases reached patients worldwide. Banting and Macleod were given the Nobel Prize in 1923 and shared their money with Best and Collip. The discoverers sold the patent to the university for a dollar each so that no one could control the supply.

Insulin was the first protein whose amino-acid sequence was determined, in 1955, and the first human protein made by recombinant DNA, in 1978.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin).

name: Soviet Union founded
summary: The union treaty created the USSR, which lasted until [1991](event:soviet-collapse).
body:
Part of [Russian Revolution](event:russian-revolution). The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was created on 30 December 1922, when the Russian, Ukrainian, Belorussian and Transcaucasian republics signed a treaty of union at the First Congress of Soviets in Moscow. It formalised as a federation the territory the Bolsheviks had reconquered in the [civil war](event:russian-revolution).

The constitution that followed in 1924 gave each republic its own government and a nominal right to secede, but every one of them was governed by a single, centralised Communist Party, and that party rather than the federal structure was where power lay. Lenin and Stalin had argued over the design: Stalin wanted the republics absorbed into Russia, Lenin insisted on the form of a union of equals.

The union began with four republics and grew to fifteen, taking in Central Asia, the Baltic states and Moldavia. Lenin died in January 1924, and by the end of the decade Stalin had defeated his rivals and begun forced collectivisation and the five-year plans.

The USSR became one of the two superpowers after [1945](event:ww2) and dissolved on the last day of [1991](event:soviet-collapse).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union).

name: Great Kanto earthquake
summary: An earthquake of about magnitude 8 destroyed Tokyo and Yokohama; between 105,000 and 142,000 people died, most of them in the fires.
body:
The Great Kantō earthquake struck the Kantō plain at 11:58 on the morning of 1 September 1923, with a magnitude of about 8 and an epicentre in Sagami Bay south-west of Tokyo. Estimates of the dead and missing run from 105,000 to 142,000. It is the most destructive earthquake in Japanese history.

The shaking flattened much of Yokohama and large districts of Tokyo, but the fires did most of the killing. It was lunchtime and cooking fires were lit across two cities of wood and paper; gas mains broke, water mains broke with them, and a typhoon passing off the coast drove the wind. In Honjo, in eastern Tokyo, tens of thousands of people who had gathered with their belongings in an open army clothing depot were killed by a fire whirl in a few minutes.

In the days that followed, rumours that Koreans were poisoning wells and setting fires spread through the ruins, and vigilante groups, with police and soldiers among them, murdered an estimated 6,000 Korean residents, along with Chinese labourers and Japanese socialists.

Reconstruction remade Tokyo with wider streets, parks as firebreaks and reinforced concrete, and it cost so much that it strained Japanese public finances for the rest of the decade.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1923_Great_Kant%C5%8D_earthquake).

name: Scopes Monkey Trial
summary: A Tennessee schoolteacher was prosecuted for teaching evolution, putting [Darwin's theory](event:origin-species) on trial before a national radio audience.
body:
John Scopes, a young teacher in Dayton, Tennessee, was tried in July 1925 for teaching human evolution in a state school, in breach of the Butler Act passed that spring. He was convicted and fined $100.

The case was arranged rather than stumbled into: the American Civil Liberties Union advertised for a teacher willing to test the law, and Dayton businessmen saw an opportunity to put their town on the map. It became a national spectacle when William Jennings Bryan, three times a presidential candidate, joined the prosecution and Clarence Darrow, the best-known defence lawyer in the country, took the other side. It was the first American trial broadcast live on radio, and hundreds of reporters attended.

The judge refused to hear expert evidence on evolution, so Darrow called Bryan himself as an expert on the Bible and questioned him for two hours on the literal truth of Genesis. Scopes was convicted the next day. The Tennessee Supreme Court set the fine aside on a technicality and the law itself stood until 1967.

The trial fixed a division in American life between scientific consensus on [Darwin's theory](event:origin-species) and religious conviction. Publishers quietly dropped evolution from school textbooks for a generation afterwards.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopes_trial).

name: British General Strike
summary: British coal miners struck over wage cuts, joined by millions of other workers in the only general strike in British history.
body:
The General Strike of 1926 was called by the Trades Union Congress on 3 May in support of coal miners facing longer hours and lower wages, and called off nine days later on 12 May. Around 1.7 million workers came out, among them railwaymen, dockers, printers and workers in transport and heavy industry, in the only general strike in British history.

Coal was the industry in crisis. The return to the gold standard in 1925 at the pre-war exchange rate had made British exports expensive, and the owners' answer was to cut costs at the pit. A government subsidy held the position for nine months while a royal commission reported; when it ran out, the owners locked the miners out.

The government had used that time to prepare. Volunteers and troops kept food moving, the BBC and the government's own newspaper carried its account, and the strike stayed peaceful and solid but achieved nothing. The TUC ended it without any concession for the miners, who stayed out until November and went back on worse terms.

The Trade Disputes Act of 1927 made sympathetic strikes illegal. The defeat pushed the labour movement towards parliamentary politics through the Labour Party.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1926_United_Kingdom_general_strike).

name: Lindbergh's transatlantic flight
summary: Charles Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis alone from New York to Paris in 33 hours, the first solo non-stop crossing of the Atlantic.
body:
Charles Lindbergh flew alone from New York to Paris on 20–21 May 1927 in the *Spirit of St. Louis*, a single-engined monoplane built to his specification, covering about 5,800 kilometres in 33 hours and 30 minutes. It was the first solo non-stop flight across the Atlantic, and it won the $25,000 Orteig Prize.

Others had crossed the ocean by air before (Alcock and Brown flew Newfoundland to Ireland in 1919), but the New York to Paris route was longer, and six men had died attempting it in the months before Lindbergh went. He flew without a radio and without a forward window, navigating by dead reckoning, and fought sleep for the second half of the flight.

A crowd estimated at 100,000 broke onto the field at Le Bourget when he landed. He became one of the most famous men in the world, and the flight is usually credited with turning American opinion towards aviation: airmail contracts, airline investment and passenger numbers all rose sharply after it.

His infant son was kidnapped and murdered in 1932 in a case that fixed public attention for years, and his prominence in the isolationist America First Committee before [1941](event:pearl-harbor), together with his praise for German aviation, cost him much of his standing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lindbergh).

name: The Jazz Singer
summary: The first commercially successful film with synchronised sound; silent production in the United States had stopped within about three years.
body:
*The Jazz Singer*, released by Warner Bros. on 6 October 1927, was the first feature-length film with synchronised recorded speech and song to be a commercial success. Al Jolson's few lines of dialogue and six songs, recorded on Vitaphone discs played in step with the projector, ended the silent era within about three years.

The film is otherwise a silent picture with intertitles, and sound films had been demonstrated for decades; what it proved was that audiences would pay for them. Warner Bros., a small studio, had gambled on the technology, and its success forced every other studio to convert. Theatres worldwide were wired for sound at great expense over the following years, and by 1930 silent production had effectively stopped in the United States.

Careers ended for actors whose voices or accents did not suit, and the visual comedians who had built the silent form struggled; camera work became static for a time while microphones dictated where actors could stand. Silent film had been an international commodity (new intertitles were all a foreign market needed) and sound tied a film to its language, which strengthened the position of English-language cinema and gave rise to dubbing and subtitling.

The film is also remembered for Jolson's blackface performance, a convention of the American stage of the time that is now widely regarded as racist.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Singer).

name: Invention of television
summary: Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first all-electronic television image in 1927, the basis of every television system since.
body:
On 7 September 1927, in a San Francisco laboratory, the twenty-one-year-old Philo Farnsworth transmitted a single straight line to a receiver using an all-electronic system of his own design. It was the first television picture made without any moving mechanical parts, and the principle behind every television set built since.

Mechanical systems came first: John Logie Baird demonstrated moving silhouettes in London in 1925 and a working televised image in 1926, using a spinning perforated disc. They were dim, small and coarse, and could not be scaled up. Farnsworth's image dissector scanned the scene with an electron beam instead, at speeds no disc could reach.

Vladimir Zworykin, working for Westinghouse and then RCA, was developing the rival iconoscope camera tube over the same years. RCA fought Farnsworth's patents for a decade and lost, and paid him licence fees. The two lines of work between them produced the electronic camera and the cathode-ray display.

Regular electronic broadcasting began in Britain in 1936 and in the United States in 1939, and [war](event:ww2) then suspended it. Television spread into most American and European homes during the 1950s and became the medium through which politics, news and mass entertainment reached the public for the rest of the century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_television).

name: Discovery of penicillin
summary: Alexander Fleming noticed that a stray mould killed bacteria on a forgotten culture plate.
body:
In September 1928, at St Mary's Hospital in London, Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find that a culture plate of staphylococci had been contaminated by a mould, and that the bacteria around the mould had dissolved. The mould was *Penicillium notatum*, and the substance it made was the first antibiotic.

Fleming published in 1929 and identified what the substance could kill, but could not purify or concentrate it, and the work lapsed for a decade. In 1939 a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain took it up, extracted enough to test, and showed in 1940 that it cured mice infected with a lethal dose of streptococci. The first human patient, treated in 1941, improved and then died when the supply ran out.

Britain in wartime had no capacity to make it in quantity, so Florey took the work to the United States, where deep-tank fermentation with a more productive strain (found on a supermarket melon) raised output enormously. Enough was made to treat the Allied wounded from 1944.

Penicillin cured infections that had regularly killed: septicaemia, pneumonia, meningitis, gonorrhoea, wound infection. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945, and Fleming used his lecture to warn that misuse would breed resistant bacteria, which it has.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penicillin).

name: Great Depression
summary: The deepest economic collapse of the industrial age: a quarter of American workers unemployed, world trade down by two thirds.
body:
The Great Depression was the worldwide economic collapse of the 1930s, the deepest and longest of the industrial age. It began in the United States around the [Wall Street crash](event:wall-street-crash) of October 1929 and spread through trade and the gold standard to almost every country. American output fell by about a third and unemployment reached roughly a quarter of the workforce; world trade fell by around two thirds.

There is no single agreed cause. Contemporary weaknesses included an American boom financed by credit and stock speculation, agricultural prices already depressed through the 1920s, war debts and reparations that made international payments fragile, and banks with no deposit insurance and little supervision. The downturn deepened with the response to it: central banks defended the gold standard with high interest rates when the economy needed the opposite, thousands of banks failed and destroyed the credit and savings behind them, and the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930 helped set off a round of retaliation that shrank trade further.
