Recovery came earliest to the countries that left gold first and could then loosen money (Britain in 1931, the United States in 1933). In the United States, Roosevelt's New Deal brought bank regulation, deposit insurance, public works, farm price support and, in 1935, social security. It did not end the slump, which returned in 1937–38 and was finished by rearmament and [war](event:ww2).

The Depression discredited liberal economics, expanded what states were expected to do for their citizens, and gave authoritarian movements their opening in Europe and Japan, in Germany above all, where the Nazi vote rose with unemployment and [Hitler took power](event:hitler-chancellor) in 1933.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression).

steps.name: The banking panics
steps.page:
Waves of bank failures ran through the United States from the autumn of 1930: the collapse of the Bank of United States in New York that December, further panics in 1931 and 1932, and a final one in the winter of 1932–33 in which states closed their banks one after another.

Around 9,000 banks failed. There was no deposit insurance, so their depositors simply lost their savings, and the credit that surviving banks would extend contracted with them. The money supply fell by about a third between 1929 and 1933. Later economists identified that contraction as the mechanism that turned a recession into a depression.

steps.name: Britain leaves gold
steps.page:
The failure of Austria's Creditanstalt in May 1931 set off a banking crisis across central Europe and a run on sterling. On 21 September Britain suspended the gold standard and let the pound float; it fell by about a quarter.

Two dozen countries followed within a year. Leaving gold freed a government to lower interest rates and expand credit instead of defending a fixed exchange rate, and the countries that left earliest recovered earliest, one of the clearest findings in the economic history of the Depression.

steps.name: The bank holiday and the New Deal
steps.page:
Roosevelt took office on 4 March 1933 with the banking system closed in most states. He declared a national bank holiday two days later, and Congress passed emergency legislation allowing sound banks to reopen under federal inspection; when they did, deposits came back.

The hundred days that followed created deposit insurance, securities regulation, farm price support, the Tennessee Valley Authority and public works and relief employment on a large scale. The United States left the gold standard in April. The New Deal did not end the Depression, but it stopped the collapse and rebuilt the machinery of finance.

steps.name: The recession of 1937
steps.page:
By 1937 output was approaching its 1929 level, and the administration cut spending to balance the budget while the Federal Reserve raised bank reserve requirements. The economy fell back sharply: industrial production dropped by about a third in nine months and unemployment rose again by several million.

Spending resumed in 1938 and the recovery with it. Full employment returned only with war orders. The sequence was later read as evidence for the argument John Maynard Keynes published in 1936.

name: Wall Street crash
summary: The New York stock market lost about a third of its value in weeks in October 1929.
body:
Part of [Great Depression](event:great-depression). The Wall Street crash of October 1929 was the sudden collapse of American share prices that ended a decade-long bull market. The New York market fell about 11 per cent on Black Thursday, 24 October, and after a weekend of alarm fell 13 per cent on Monday the 28th and 12 per cent on Tuesday the 29th, the heaviest trading day recorded to that point.

Prices had risen through the 1920s well past what company earnings supported, driven by borrowing: shares could be bought on margin with a tenth of the price in cash, so a small fall wiped out the buyer's stake and forced a sale, which pushed prices down further. The Dow Jones index had peaked at 381 on 3 September 1929. It reached its floor at 41 in July 1932, a fall of 89 per cent, and did not regain the 1929 level until 1954.

The crash did not by itself cause the [Great Depression](event:great-depression), and most Americans owned no shares, but it destroyed a great deal of wealth and the confidence to spend, lend and invest. Banks that had lent against securities were weakened, and the panics that followed over the next three years did the deeper damage.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_Crash_of_1929).

name: The Dust Bowl
summary: Drought and ploughed-up prairie grass turned the southern Great Plains into moving dunes, displacing hundreds of thousands.
body:
Part of [Great Depression](event:great-depression). The Dust Bowl was the series of severe dust storms that struck the southern Great Plains (western Kansas, the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, eastern Colorado and New Mexico) through the drought years of the 1930s.

Wheat prices and mechanised ploughs had brought millions of hectares of native grassland under cultivation in the preceding decades. The grass had held the soil and its moisture; the ploughed ground did not. When drought settled over the region from 1930, the topsoil dried, and the wind took it. Storms rolled black clouds hundreds of metres high across the plains, buried fences and machinery, and carried dust as far as Chicago and the ships off the Atlantic coast. The worst, on 14 April 1935, is remembered as Black Sunday.

Perhaps 2.5 million people left the plains states during the decade, many for California, where they were called Okies and met with hostility; the migration is the subject of Steinbeck's *The Grapes of Wrath* and Dorothea Lange's photographs. Those who stayed faced dust pneumonia and ruined land.

The federal response created the Soil Conservation Service in 1935 and taught contour ploughing, crop rotation, cover crops and shelter belts. The rains returned at the end of the decade.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_Bowl).

name: Gandhi's Salt March
summary: Gandhi walked 385 km to the sea to make salt in defiance of the British monopoly, launching mass civil disobedience.
body:
Part of [British Raj](event:british-raj). [Gandhi](item:mohandas-gandhi) walked 385 kilometres from his ashram at Sabarmati to the coast at Dandi between 12 March and 5 April 1930, and on the morning of the 6th picked up a lump of natural salt from the beach, breaking the government's salt monopoly. It began the civil disobedience campaign of 1930–34.

Salt was chosen deliberately. It was taxed, its private manufacture was illegal, and everybody needed it, so the law bore on the poorest and could be broken by anyone. The march was slow and public, with journalists and newsreel cameras following it through village after village, and it drew national and international press coverage.

Mass salt-making, boycotts of foreign cloth and liquor, and refusal to pay taxes followed across India. About 60,000 people were arrested, Gandhi among them, and at Dharasana in May police beat unresisting volunteers as they advanced in lines, and accounts of the beating were cabled worldwide.

The immediate political gain was small, and the Round Table Conference that followed produced nothing. The campaign showed that non-cooperation could be organised on a national scale, and it drew international attention to the independence movement. Gandhi's methods were studied by later movements, among them the [American civil rights campaign](event:civil-rights).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_March).

name: Japanese invasion of Manchuria
summary: Japanese forces seized Manchuria from China in 1931 and set up the state of Manchukuo; the League of Nations took no action.
body:
On the night of 18 September 1931 officers of Japan's Kwantung Army set off a small explosion on the South Manchuria Railway near Mukden, blamed it on Chinese soldiers, and used it as the pretext to occupy the whole of Manchuria. The Japanese government in Tokyo had not authorised the operation and proved unable to stop it.

Manchuria was worth taking: coal, iron, soya and land, and a buffer against the Soviet Union. Within five months Japanese forces held a territory larger than France and Germany together, and in March 1932 they proclaimed it the state of Manchukuo, with the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as its figurehead.

China appealed to the League of Nations. The Lytton commission reported in 1932 that Japan had been the aggressor and that Manchukuo was not a genuine independent state; the League adopted the report, and Japan walked out of the League in March 1933 rather than accept it. No sanctions were imposed and no force was contemplated.

The episode showed that the post-war settlement would not be enforced against a determined great power. Italy in [Abyssinia](event:abyssinia-invasion) and Germany in the Rhineland followed the same reading. For Japan it was the first step of a continental war that became the [invasion of China proper](event:sino-japanese-war) in 1937.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_invasion_of_Manchuria).

name: Hitler appointed Chancellor of Germany
summary: President Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler Chancellor, believing he could be controlled and that the appointment would end Germany's political paralysis.
body:
Paul von Hindenburg, president of Germany, appointed Adolf Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933 at the head of a coalition cabinet in which the Nazis held only three of eleven posts. The conservatives who arranged it believed they had hired him and could control him.

The Nazi party had taken 37 per cent of the vote in July 1932, the largest share in the Reichstag, and fallen back to 33 per cent in November; it was losing money and members, and Hitler had refused any office but the chancellorship. Germany had been governed by presidential emergency decree for three years, with six million unemployed and street fighting between paramilitaries. Franz von Papen, who wanted back into office, persuaded Hindenburg that a Hitler cabinet hemmed in by conservatives was the way out.

The Reichstag fire of 27 February gave the pretext for a decree suspending civil liberties and arresting the Communist deputies. Elections held under those conditions on 5 March still gave the Nazis only 44 per cent, but with the Communists excluded the [Enabling Act](event:enabling-act) passed on 23 March, and Hitler could legislate without parliament or president.

Within six months the other parties were dissolved or banned, the trade unions were absorbed, the states lost their governments, and the first camps held tens of thousands of political prisoners. When Hindenburg died in August 1934 Hitler merged the presidency with his own office and the army swore an oath to him personally.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machtergreifung).

name: Enabling Act in Nazi Germany
summary: The Reichstag voted to let Hitler's cabinet make laws without parliament, ending parliamentary government in Germany.
body:
The Enabling Act was passed by the German Reichstag on 23 March 1933 by 444 votes to 94. It allowed the cabinet (in practice [Hitler](event:hitler-chancellor)) to enact laws without the parliament or the president, including laws that departed from the constitution, for four years.

It was a constitutional amendment and needed a two-thirds majority of a quorate house. That was arranged rather than won: the 81 Communist deputies had been arrested or driven underground after the Reichstag fire and were simply counted out, some Social Democrats were also in custody, and the sitting was held in a hall lined with SA men. The Centre Party, whose votes decided it, accepted a written promise of the president's continuing rights and the position of the churches that was never delivered. Only the remaining Social Democrats voted against, after their leader Otto Wels spoke against the bill to Hitler's face.

The act removed the last legal obstacle. Within months the other parties were banned or dissolved, the civil service was purged of Jews and opponents, the states were brought under central control, and the trade unions were replaced by a state labour front. It was renewed in 1937, 1939 and 1943.

Parliamentary government in Germany ended with this vote. The dictatorship it legalised governed until the German defeat in [1945](event:ww2).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enabling_Act_of_1933).

name: Italian invasion of Abyssinia
summary: Mussolini's forces invaded Ethiopia, one of only two African states that had kept their independence, and used chemical weapons against its army and civilians.
body:
Italy invaded Ethiopia (then usually called Abyssinia) on 3 October 1935 without a declaration of war, and annexed it the following May. Ethiopia was a member of the League of Nations and one of only two African states never colonised.

Mussolini wanted an empire, and revenge for the Italian defeat at Adwa in 1896. Around half a million men, with aircraft, armour and artillery, advanced from Eritrea and Italian Somaliland against an army with few modern weapons. Italian forces used mustard gas from aircraft and in bombs against soldiers, civilians, villages and Red Cross hospitals, in breach of the Geneva Protocol Italy had signed. Addis Ababa fell on 5 May 1936 and Haile Selassie went into exile; a guerrilla resistance continued until British and Ethiopian forces restored him in 1941.

The League declared Italy the aggressor and imposed economic sanctions, but left out oil, coal and steel and did not close the Suez Canal to Italian shipping. Britain and France meanwhile drafted the Hoare-Laval pact to hand Italy most of what it had invaded to keep it out of German hands; the leak of it brought down both foreign ministers and destroyed what credibility the sanctions had.

Haile Selassie appealed to the League in person in June 1936, telling the assembly "It is us today. It will be you tomorrow." Hitler reoccupied the Rhineland in March 1936 while the powers were occupied with Ethiopia.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War).

name: Spanish Civil War
summary: Franco's nationalists, backed by Germany and Italy, defeated the Republic in a war that served as a rehearsal for [the world war](event:ww2).
body:
The Spanish Civil War was fought from July 1936 to April 1939 between the elected Republican government and a nationalist rebellion of much of the army, led from 1936 by Francisco Franco. The rebels won, and Franco ruled Spain until his death in 1975. Around half a million people died, a large share of them executed behind the lines by both sides.

The rising followed years of polarisation over land, the church, the army and regional autonomy, and the narrow victory of a Popular Front coalition in February 1936. The coup succeeded in much of the west and north and failed in Madrid, Barcelona and the industrial north, which split the country and turned a coup into a war.

Foreign intervention decided it. Germany and Italy sent aircraft, tanks, artillery and men to Franco (the German Condor Legion bombed Guernica in April 1937), while Britain and France organised a non-intervention agreement that the Soviet Union, which supplied the Republic, and the Axis powers both ignored. Some 35,000 volunteers came from over fifty countries in the International Brigades. The Republic was also divided against itself, with communists, anarchists and the POUM fighting each other in Barcelona in 1937.

Madrid fell on 28 March 1939 and the war ended on 1 April. Five months later Germany invaded Poland. Contemporaries and historians alike have treated the war as a rehearsal for [the world war](event:ww2), in its weapons, its air attacks on cities and its politics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War).

name: Second Sino-Japanese War
summary: Japan launched a full-scale invasion of China, occupying much of the country in an eight-year war that killed millions and later merged into [World War II](event:ww2).
body:
The Second Sino-Japanese War began with a clash at the Marco Polo Bridge outside Beijing on 7 July 1937 and ended with the Japanese surrender in September 1945. It was the largest Asian war of the twentieth century, and between fifteen and twenty million Chinese died in it, the great majority of them civilians.

Japan already held Manchuria, taken in [1931](event:japan-manchuria), and expected to force a settlement in months. Instead Chiang Kai-shek committed his best divisions to the defence of Shanghai, which held for three months. Japanese forces then took Nanjing in December 1937 and massacred its population: estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to 300,000.

Japan occupied the coast, the cities and the railways; Chinese forces withdrew inland, moved what industry they could with them, and made the capital Chongqing, which was bombed for years. The Nationalist armies bore most of the conventional fighting while the Communists expanded in the countryside behind Japanese lines, the two sides in a united front that neither trusted. Japanese forces used chemical and biological weapons and ran a programme of human experimentation in Manchuria.

Japan's need for oil and rubber to sustain the war led to the occupation of French Indochina, the American embargo, and the attack on [Pearl Harbor](event:pearl-harbor), after which the Chinese war became a theatre of [the Second World War](event:ww2). China's resistance held down more than a million Japanese troops for eight years, and the civil war between Nationalists and Communists resumed as soon as it was over.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War).

name: Discovery of nuclear fission
summary: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found that uranium nuclei split when bombarded with neutrons; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained the result.
body:
In December 1938, in Berlin, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann bombarded uranium with neutrons and found barium among the products, an element little more than half the weight of uranium, which no known nuclear process could produce. Lise Meitner, who had worked with Hahn for thirty years and had fled to Sweden that summer, and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out the explanation over Christmas: the uranium nucleus had split in two.

They calculated that each split would release about 200 million electron volts, millions of times the energy of a chemical reaction between the same atoms, drawn from the difference in mass between the nucleus and its fragments. Frisch borrowed the word *fission* from biology and confirmed the energy release experimentally in January 1939.

The implication was recognised at once: if the splitting also released spare neutrons, a chain reaction was possible, and with it both a power source and a bomb. Within months laboratories had confirmed that it did. Refugee physicists, fearing that Germany would build the weapon first, persuaded [Einstein](item:albert-einstein) to sign a letter to President Roosevelt in August 1939.

Enrico Fermi's team produced the first controlled chain reaction in Chicago in December 1942, and the [Manhattan Project](event:trinity) followed. Hahn alone received the Nobel Prize for chemistry for the discovery in 1944; Meitner's exclusion is one of the more discussed omissions in the history of the prize.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fission).

name: World War II
summary: The deadliest conflict in history: some 70–85 million dead, fought across every ocean and most continents.
body:
World War II was fought from 1939 to 1945 between the Allies (chiefly the Soviet Union, the United States, Britain and China) and the Axis powers of Germany, Japan and Italy. It was the deadliest conflict in history: estimates of the dead run from 70 to 85 million, most of them civilians, killed in bombing, massacre, famine, disease and genocide as well as in battle.

The war in Europe began when Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 and Britain and France declared war two days later. In Asia, Japan had been at war in [China](event:sino-japanese-war) since 1937. Germany overran Denmark, Norway, the Low Countries and France in the spring of 1940, failed to win the air battle over [Britain](event:battle-britain) that summer, and then turned east: [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa) opened the largest land campaign ever fought on 22 June 1941. Japan's attack on [Pearl Harbor](event:pearl-harbor) in December brought the United States in, and Germany declared war on it four days later.

The Axis reached its furthest extent in 1942 and lost the initiative that autumn and winter at [Midway](event:midway), at El Alamein and at [Stalingrad](event:stalingrad). From then the war was a matter of Allied industrial weight and manpower closing in from three directions: the Red Army westward, the British and American armies through North Africa, Italy and then [Normandy](event:d-day), and the American advance across the Pacific. Strategic bombing destroyed the cities of Germany and Japan.

Behind the German front, the occupation regime carried out the [Holocaust](event:holocaust), murdering six million Jews, and killed millions more Soviet prisoners, Poles, Roma and disabled people. Japanese occupation forces killed on a comparable scale in China and South-East Asia.

Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945, weeks after Soviet troops took Berlin. Japan surrendered after the [atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki](event:hiroshima), the first use of the weapon the [Trinity test](event:trinity) had proved a month earlier, and the Soviet declaration of war in Manchuria; the formal surrender was signed on 2 September 1945.

The war left the United States and the Soviet Union as the only great powers, divided Europe between them for forty years in the [Cold War](event:cold-war), produced the United Nations, and broke the hold of the European empires on Asia and Africa.

The steps below follow the war from Britain's air defence to the Japanese surrender.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II).

name: Battle of Britain
summary: The RAF held off the Luftwaffe in the first campaign fought entirely in the air, ending the threat of invasion.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The Battle of Britain was the air campaign fought over Britain and the Channel between July and October 1940, in which the Royal Air Force defeated the German attempt to win command of the air. It was the first campaign in history fought entirely by aircraft, and the first defeat of the German armed forces in the war.

Germany needed air superiority before it could attempt a seaborne invasion. The Luftwaffe attacked shipping in the Channel, then the airfields and the radar stations of Fighter Command, and in September switched to bombing London and other cities, which relieved the pressure on the airfields when they were suffering most.

British advantages did not show in the numbers of aircraft. The Dowding system linked radar stations, the Observer Corps and telephone lines into a single ground-controlled network that put fighters where the bombers were instead of leaving them to patrol. Damaged aircraft came down over home territory and their pilots could fly again; German aircrew who baled out were lost. Fighter production ran ahead of losses through the summer.

On 17 September Hitler postponed the invasion indefinitely. Night raids on British cities (the Blitz) continued into May 1941 and killed some 40,000 civilians, but the air battle had been decided.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain).

name: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: A Japanese carrier strike on the US Pacific Fleet brought the United States into the war.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). On the morning of Sunday 7 December 1941, aircraft from six Japanese carriers attacked the United States Pacific Fleet at its base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. Some 2,400 Americans were killed. The attack brought the United States into the Second World War.

Japan's war in [China](event:sino-japanese-war) had brought American oil and steel embargoes that would have run its armed forces down within two years. Rather than withdraw, its government chose to seize the resources of South-East Asia and to remove the fleet that could interfere. The attack came without a declaration of war, in two waves of 353 aircraft launched from 350 kilometres to the north.

Four battleships were sunk and four more damaged, along with cruisers, destroyers and nearly 200 aircraft. The Japanese lost 29 aircraft. The attack left the main targets of a longer war untouched: the American aircraft carriers were at sea, and the base's fuel tanks, dry docks and repair shops were left standing, so Pearl Harbor remained usable as a fleet base.

Congress declared war on Japan the next day; Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on 11 December, which joined the war in Asia to the war in Europe. Japanese landings in Malaya, the Philippines and the Dutch East Indies began within hours of the attack.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor).

name: The Holocaust
summary: Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners and political opponents.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The Holocaust was the genocide of European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. Between 1941 and 1945 about six million Jews were murdered, some two-thirds of the Jewish population of Europe, most of them in 1942, the peak year of the killing.

It was built on eight years of escalating persecution. After 1933 some 1,500 laws and decrees stripped German Jews of professions, property, citizenship and civil rights; the pogrom of November 1938 destroyed synagogues and businesses across the country. After the invasion of Poland in 1939, Jews there were confined in ghettos, of which Warsaw and Łódź were the largest, where hunger and disease killed hundreds of thousands.

The mass killing began with the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. Einsatzgruppen (mobile squads following the army), police battalions and local auxiliaries shot between 1.5 and 2 million people into pits behind the front. At the Wannsee conference in January 1942 officials coordinated the deportation of the Jews of the whole continent, and purpose-built extermination camps at Bełżec, Sobibór, Treblinka, Chełmno, Majdanek and Auschwitz-Birkenau killed arriving transports with gas. Auschwitz alone accounted for about a million deaths. As the fronts closed in, the surviving prisoners were driven west on foot in death marches in which tens of thousands more died.

Millions of others were killed in the same system: 3.3 million Soviet prisoners of war, Polish and Soviet civilians, Roma, disabled people murdered in the T4 programme, political prisoners and homosexuals.

The word *genocide* was coined in 1944 to describe what was being done, and the Genocide Convention followed in 1948.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust).

name: Operation Barbarossa
summary: Germany invaded the Soviet Union along a 2,900 km front, the largest invasion in history.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). Operation Barbarossa was the German invasion of the Soviet Union, launched on 22 June 1941 along a front of some 2,900 kilometres from the Baltic to the Black Sea. About 3.8 million Axis troops took part, the largest invasion force ever assembled, and it opened the war's largest and deadliest theatre.

Hitler's aims were the destruction of the Soviet state, the seizure of its grain and oil, and the clearing of the western Soviet Union for German settlement. It was planned as a war of annihilation, with the Commissar Order and the mass starvation of prisoners written into it. Three army groups advanced on Leningrad, Moscow and Kiev. Soviet forces, deployed forward and forbidden to withdraw, were encircled in a series of enormous pockets and lost more than three million men taken prisoner in six months.

The campaign nonetheless failed. The Soviet state did not collapse, factories were evacuated east and kept producing, and German losses, supply lines and the autumn mud slowed the advance until the offensive stalled within sight of Moscow. A Soviet counter-offensive on 5 December drove the Germans back from the capital.

The invasion killed and displaced millions and left the Wehrmacht in a war of attrition. Mass shootings by the Einsatzgruppen behind the front began with it, the first phase of the [Holocaust](event:holocaust).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa).

steps.name: The border battles (June)
steps.page:
Three army groups crossed the 1939 demarcation line before dawn on 22 June 1941 and broke through the covering forces of the western Soviet military districts within days. Army Group Centre closed two rings behind Białystok and Minsk and took some 324,000 prisoners; Army Group North crossed the Dvina into Latvia; Army Group South met the heaviest armour of the campaign around Dubno and Brody.

Positions the advance bypassed were not always reduced. The garrison of [Brest Fortress](item:brest-fortress), surrounded on the first morning, held out inside the German rear for a week.

steps.name: Smolensk (July–September)
steps.page:
Through July and August Army Group Centre fought its way up the Moscow highway. The [battle of Smolensk](item:smolensk-1941) cost the Red Army a further 300,000 prisoners, but it absorbed two months of the campaign's good weather and the Soviet counterattacks at Yelnya recovered ground for the first time since the invasion began.

In the south the [Uman pocket](item:uman-pocket) destroyed two Soviet armies in August. In the north the ring closed on Leningrad, cut off by land on 8 September; the Baltic Fleet had already run the [evacuation of Tallinn](item:tallinn-evacuation) through minefields at the end of August.

steps.name: Kiev (September)
steps.page:
In September Panzer Group 2 turned south off the Moscow axis and met Panzer Group 1 east of Kiev, closing the largest encirclement of the war around the Soviet South-Western Front. Some 665,000 men were taken.

The turn secured the Ukraine and the approaches to the Donbass, and it cost the advance on Moscow a month of the campaigning season, a decision much argued over since.

steps.name: Typhoon (October–December)
steps.page:
Operation Typhoon opened on 30 September. Double encirclements at Vyazma and Bryansk took a further 673,000 prisoners and left the road to Moscow thinly held; then the autumn rains turned it to mud and the December frosts caught an army that had been equipped for a summer campaign.

The leading formations came within about 30 km of the capital, at Krasnaya Polyana, and stopped there.

steps.name: The counteroffensive (December)
steps.page:
On 5 December the Red Army attacked with divisions brought from the Far East, and over the following weeks pushed the front back between 100 and 250 km along the Moscow axis. Rostov had already been given up on 29 November, the first city the Wehrmacht abandoned.

Barbarossa's object, the destruction of the Soviet Union in a single campaign, had failed. The war in the east ran on for another three and a half years. See [World War II](event:ww2).

name: Białystok–Minsk encirclement
summary: Army Group Centre's panzer pincers closed east of Minsk in the war's first fortnight, taking some 324,000 prisoners.
body:
Part of [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa). The Białystok–Minsk encirclement was the first great pocket of the invasion. Guderian's and Hoth's panzer groups drove past the Soviet armies on the frontier from 22 June 1941 and met east of Minsk on 27 June, closing a ring around most of the Soviet Western Front while the German infantry armies formed a second, inner ring around Białystok.

The Soviet defence had been deployed close to the border and ordered to counter-attack rather than withdraw, which left it inside the pincers before its commanders understood what was happening. Communications broke down almost immediately; several armies fought without orders or supply.

Resistance in the pockets ended by 8 July. The Germans counted some 324,000 prisoners, 3,300 tanks and 1,800 guns. The commander of the Western Front, Dmitry Pavlov, was recalled to Moscow, tried and shot.

Minsk was 350 kilometres from the frontier and had been reached in six days. The scale of the victory persuaded the German command that the campaign was already decided, and it set the pattern for [Smolensk](event:smolensk-1941), [Uman](event:uman-pocket) and [Kiev](event:kiev-pocket).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bia%C5%82ystok%E2%80%93Minsk).

name: Defence of Brest Fortress
summary: The frontier fortress on the Bug was surrounded on the first morning of the invasion and held out for a week inside the German rear.
body:
Part of [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa). The nineteenth-century citadel at Brest stood on the river Bug, on the demarcation line agreed between Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939. It held about 9,000 soldiers of two rifle divisions and a border guard detachment, together with some 300 families, and was surrounded within hours of the opening of the invasion on 22 June 1941.

The German 45th Infantry Division had expected to take it in a day. Cut off from any relief, the garrison fought in the cellars and ruins of the fortress against artillery, flamethrowers and dive-bombing; organised resistance ended on about 29 June, and individual soldiers held out in the casemates for weeks after that. Roughly 2,000 defenders were killed and 6,800 captured; the attackers lost 429 dead, an unusually high figure for a single division in the first week of the campaign.

The defence had no effect on the timetable of the advance, which went round it. It became instead one of the first Soviet accounts of the war that could be told as a stand rather than as a retreat: the fortress was made a Hero Fortress in 1965, and the story that it held out for a month, though not supported by the evidence, is the version that entered public memory.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_of_Brest_Fortress).

name: Battle of Smolensk
summary: Two months of fighting on the road to Moscow cost the Red Army some 300,000 prisoners and delayed the German advance.
body:
Part of [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa). The Battle of Smolensk was fought from 10 July to 10 September 1941 on the upper Dnieper, on the direct road from the frontier to Moscow. Army Group Centre closed a pocket around Smolensk in the second half of July and took some 300,000 prisoners, but it took two months to finish a battle it had expected to fight in days.

Fresh Soviet armies were fed in from the reserve as fast as they could be raised, and counter-attacked continuously along the highway. At Yelnya, a salient east of Smolensk, they forced the first German withdrawal of the war at the beginning of September.

Red Army losses were very heavy, and the Germans lost time: their mobile divisions were worn down, their infantry left far behind, and the decision was taken at the end of August to turn the armour south into Ukraine for the [Kiev encirclement](event:kiev-pocket) rather than press on to Moscow. The advance on the capital did not resume until 30 September, with the autumn rains a fortnight away.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Smolensk_(1941)).

name: Uman encirclement
summary: Two Soviet armies were surrounded south-west of Kiev in August 1941, losing about 103,000 men taken prisoner.
body:
Part of [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa). The Uman encirclement destroyed two Soviet armies in the black-earth country south-west of Kiev in the summer of 1941. Army Group South's 1st Panzer Group drove south-east behind the retreating Soviet South-Western Front from mid-July while the 17th Army pushed east, and the two closed a ring near Uman in the first days of August.

Inside it were the Soviet 6th and 12th Armies and the 2nd Mechanized Corps, fighting under a combined command that had been formed a week earlier as the position collapsed. Resistance in the pocket ended on 8 August. Around 100,000 men were taken prisoner, along with both army commanders, four corps commanders and eleven divisional commanders, and the greater part of two armies' artillery and vehicles.

The victory opened the way east to the lower Dnieper and removed the forces that might have covered the flank of the far larger encirclement at [Kiev](event:kiev-pocket) a month later. It is one of the least-remembered of the 1941 pockets, and among the most complete.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Uman).

name: Kiev encirclement
summary: The largest encirclement in military history: about 665,000 Soviet troops were taken east of Kiev in September 1941.
body:
Part of [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa). The first battle of Kiev, in August and September 1941, produced the largest encirclement in military history. About 665,000 Soviet soldiers were taken prisoner when the German pincers closed east of the city.

Hitler halted the advance on Moscow at the end of August and turned Guderian's panzer group south from the Smolensk axis, against the objections of his army command. Kleist's group drove north from its bridgehead over the Dnieper at Kremenchuk, and the two met at Lokhvytsia, 200 kilometres east of Kiev, on 16 September. Four Soviet armies of the South-Western Front were inside the ring; Stalin had refused permission to withdraw them until it was too late, and the front's commander, Mikhail Kirponos, was killed trying to break out.

Kiev fell on 19 September and organised resistance in the pocket ended by 26 September. The Germans took Ukraine's industry and grain and secured their southern flank.

The price was five weeks. When Operation Typhoon opened against Moscow on 30 September, the mud of the autumn thaw was a month away and the winter behind it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kiev_(1941)).

name: Evacuation of Tallinn
summary: The Baltic Fleet ran its ships out of Tallinn through minefields and air attack in August 1941, losing about a fifth of them and some 15,000 people.
body:
Part of [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa). With Army Group North astride Estonia and the city about to fall, the Soviet Baltic Fleet abandoned its main base at Tallinn on 27 August 1941 and made for Kronstadt, 300 kilometres east. Some 225 warships, auxiliaries and transports sailed, carrying the garrison, wounded, party officials and civilians.

The route ran along a narrow swept channel past Cape Juminda, where German and Finnish forces had laid several thousand mines earlier in the month, and lay under German air attack for its whole length with almost no fighter cover. Mines accounted for most of the losses and aircraft for the rest: some 50 to 60 vessels were sunk over three days, most of them transports crowded with troops. Russian accounts put the dead at about 15,000; some estimates are higher.

About 160 ships reached Kronstadt. Their guns and crews reinforced the naval artillery that helped hold the perimeter through the [siege of Leningrad](event:leningrad-siege), which closed a fortnight later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_evacuation_of_Tallinn).

name: Siege of Leningrad
summary: Army Group North cut the city off in September 1941; some 800,000 civilians died before the blockade was lifted.
body:
Part of [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa). The siege of Leningrad began on 8 September 1941, when German forces took Shlisselburg and cut the last land route into the city, and was not fully lifted until 27 January 1944, 872 days later. Around 800,000 civilians died, the great majority of starvation, in the deadliest blockade of a city in modern history.

Hitler's intention was not to take Leningrad but to starve it. Finnish forces closed the approaches from the north; the German ring held the south. Nearly three million people were inside it, and the food stores burned in the first air raids. The bread ration fell to 125 grams a day in the winter of 1941–42, people ate wallpaper paste and leather, and cases of cannibalism were recorded; the death rate peaked at several thousand a day in January and February 1942.

The one route in ran across Lake Ladoga, by barge in summer and by lorry over the ice in winter, under artillery and air attack. It brought in food and fuel and carried out something over a million evacuees. Naval guns from the [Baltic Fleet](event:tallinn-evacuation) helped hold the perimeter.

A corridor was forced open in January 1943 and the siege broken a year later. The siege became a central Soviet memory of the war.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Leningrad).

name: Battle of Moscow
summary: German spearheads came within 30 km of the Kremlin before the December counter-offensive threw them back.
body:
Part of [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa). The battle of Moscow was fought from October 1941 to January 1942 for the Soviet capital. German spearheads came within about 30 kilometres of the Kremlin before a counter-offensive threw them back, in the first strategic defeat the German army suffered in the war.

Operation Typhoon opened on 30 September and destroyed the Soviet armies covering the road at Vyazma and Bryansk, taking several hundred thousand prisoners. Moscow was put under a state of siege, the government departments and much of the diplomatic corps were evacuated to Kuibyshev, and Stalin stayed. The autumn rains then turned the roads to mud and stopped the advance for three weeks; when the ground froze in November it resumed, in temperatures that fell below −30 °C against troops without winter clothing.

Zhukov held with divisions brought from the Far East, released when intelligence indicated that Japan would strike south rather than against Siberia. He counter-attacked on 5 December along the whole front and drove the Germans back 100 to 250 kilometres over the following weeks.

Hitler forbade further withdrawal and dismissed a series of commanders. The war of quick campaigns was over, and Germany was committed to a long one it was not equipped for.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Moscow).

name: Quit India Movement
summary: Congress demanded an immediate British withdrawal in August 1942; its leaders were arrested within hours and the movement was suppressed.
body:
Part of [British Raj](event:british-raj). The Quit India movement began on 8 August 1942, when the Indian National Congress passed a resolution in Bombay demanding an immediate end to British rule and [Gandhi](item:mohandas-gandhi) called for mass civil disobedience, telling Indians to "do or die".

The demand was made in the middle of the [war](event:ww2): Britain had brought India in without consulting Indian opinion, the Japanese army was at the Burmese border, and the Cripps mission had just failed to offer anything beyond dominion status after the war.

The government arrested Gandhi, Nehru and the whole Congress leadership within hours and banned the organisation. Leaderless protest turned violent in places (railway lines, telegraph wires and police stations were attacked) and was suppressed with mass arrests, public floggings and, in some districts, machine-gunning from the air. Around 100,000 people were imprisoned; over a thousand were killed. Congress was out of political life for the rest of the war, which strengthened the Muslim League's claim to speak for its own constituency.

The movement did not force the British out. It did make clear that India could not be governed after the war on the old terms, and the post-war British government conceded [independence and partition](event:indian-independence) five years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quit_India_Movement).

name: Battle of Stalingrad
summary: The German Sixth Army was encircled and destroyed in the ruined city on the Volga.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The Battle of Stalingrad was fought from August 1942 to February 1943 for the city on the Volga that carried Stalin's name. The German Sixth Army was drawn into it, encircled by a Soviet counter-offensive and destroyed. It is usually taken as the turning point of the war in Europe, and with roughly two million casualties on the two sides it is among the bloodiest battles ever fought.

The German summer offensive of 1942 aimed at the oilfields of the Caucasus, with Stalingrad as flank protection; both objectives were pursued at once with forces sufficient for one. Massive bombing reduced the city to rubble that favoured the defence, and the fighting became a house-by-house contest in which the Soviet 62nd Army held narrow strips of bank supplied across the river under fire.

On 19 November the Red Army attacked the Romanian and Hungarian armies holding the flanks north and south of the city. Operation Uranus closed a ring around some 250,000 men in four days. Hitler forbade a breakout, an airlift failed to supply the pocket, and a relief attempt was stopped 50 kilometres short.

Friedrich Paulus surrendered the remnants on 2 February 1943. About 90,000 prisoners were taken, of whom some 5,000 returned home after the war. Germany never regained the strategic initiative in the east.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad).

name: Battle of Midway
summary: American carriers sank four Japanese fleet carriers in a single day, reversing the balance in the Pacific.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The Battle of Midway was fought from 4 to 7 June 1942 near Midway Atoll in the central Pacific. American carrier aircraft sank four Japanese fleet carriers (*Akagi*, *Kaga*, *Sōryū* and *Hiryū*) for the loss of the *Yorktown*, and ended the Japanese offensive in the Pacific.

Japan intended to seize Midway and to force the surviving American carriers into a battle it expected to win. American cryptanalysts had partly broken the Japanese naval code and identified both the target and the date, which let Admiral Nimitz place three carriers north-east of the atoll in ambush.

The battle turned in a few minutes on the morning of 4 June. Japanese aircraft were being rearmed on deck between strikes when American dive bombers arrived overhead almost unopposed, the defending fighters having been drawn down to sea level by torpedo bombers that had attacked earlier and been destroyed almost to a man. Three carriers were set on fire within minutes; the fourth was found and sunk that afternoon.

Japan lost the core of its carrier force and, with it, the trained aircrew it could not replace at the rate the United States was building ships. From Midway the initiative in the Pacific passed to the Americans, who landed on Guadalcanal two months later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Midway).

name: D-Day landings
summary: The largest amphibious operation ever mounted put 156,000 Allied troops ashore in Normandy in one day.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The Normandy landings of 6 June 1944, the opening of Operation Overlord, were the largest amphibious operation ever mounted. Around 156,000 American, British and Canadian troops came ashore on five beaches in Normandy, codenamed Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, supported by some 7,000 vessels and by three airborne divisions dropped inland during the night.

The invasion had been prepared for two years and depended on air superiority, on artificial Mulberry harbours towed across the Channel, and on a deception campaign that persuaded the German command to expect the main landing at the Pas de Calais and to hold its reserves there for weeks afterwards. The assault was postponed a day by weather and went in on a marginal forecast.

Casualties on the day were about 10,000 Allied dead and wounded, more than half of them at Omaha, where the beach was overlooked by bluffs and held by a full-strength division. By nightfall the lodgements were ashore but not yet joined to one another.

The seven weeks that followed were a slow fight through the hedgerows of the bocage for Caen, Cherbourg and Saint-Lô, until the American breakout at the end of July put armour into open country. The campaign opened the Western Front that Stalin had demanded since 1941 and led to the liberation of Paris in August.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy_landings).

steps.name: 6 June
steps.page:
Airborne divisions dropped behind the invasion coast after midnight to hold its flanks. The seaborne assault began at 06:30 on the American beaches and about an hour later on the British and Canadian ones, the tides running later to the east. Utah was taken cheaply; Omaha, overlooked by bluffs and held by a full-strength division, cost the day's heaviest casualties; Rangers scaled [Pointe du Hoc](item:pointe-du-hoc) and found the battery they had come for moved inland.

By nightfall about 156,000 men were ashore in five lodgements, none of them yet joined to another.

steps.name: The beachhead
steps.page:
The landings were linked into a single bridgehead within the week, and the fighting became a contest for the bocage, small fields walled in earth banks and thorn, ground made for defence. Caen, an objective of the first day, was not taken until 9 July; an armoured thrust towards [Villers-Bocage](item:villers-bocage) on 13 June was stopped and pulled back.

A Channel gale between 19 and 22 June wrecked the American Mulberry harbour and cost more landing craft than the assault itself.

steps.name: Cherbourg
steps.page: VII Corps cut the Cotentin peninsula on 18 June and turned north for the deep-water port the campaign needed. [Cherbourg](item:cherbourg-1944) surrendered on 27 June with its harbour systematically demolished, and it did not handle cargo in quantity until the autumn.

steps.name: The breakout
steps.page: Saint-Lô fell on 19 July after a month of hedgerow fighting. Operation Cobra opened on 25 July with saturation bombing on a narrow front west of the town, broke the German line and put armour into open country, ending the battle for the beachhead.

name: Pointe du Hoc
summary: American Rangers scaled a 35-metre cliff between Utah and Omaha on 6 June 1944 to take a battery that had already been moved inland.
body:
Part of the [D-Day landings](event:d-day). Pointe du Hoc is a headland between Utah and Omaha beaches whose clifftop battery of six 155 mm guns could reach both landing areas. Three companies of the 2nd Ranger Battalion, under Lieutenant Colonel James Rudder, were given the task of destroying it.

About 225 men landed at the foot of the 35-metre cliffs at 07:10 on 6 June 1944, forty minutes late and under fire, and climbed them with rocket-fired grapnels and ladders borrowed from the London fire brigade. The position at the top had been bombed and shelled into craters, and the casemates were empty: the guns had been moved inland while the emplacements were finished. A patrol found five of them in an orchard about a kilometre away, unguarded, and disabled them with thermite grenades.

The Rangers then held the clifftop and the coast road against counter-attacks for two days, cut off, until relief arrived from Omaha on 8 June. Of the men who had landed, about 90 were still able to fight.

The action is often cited as an example of an objective that had moved before the plan reached it, and of a plan that worked anyway.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointe_du_Hoc).

name: Battle of Villers-Bocage
summary: A British armoured thrust into a gap west of Caen was stopped in the village street on 13 June 1944 and withdrawn.
body:
Part of the [D-Day landings](event:d-day). On 13 June 1944 the British 7th Armoured Division pushed through a gap in the German line towards Villers-Bocage, a road junction some 25 kilometres inland, hoping to turn the western flank of the defences holding up the advance on Caen.

Its leading squadron halted in column on the road out of the village and was destroyed in a few minutes, largely by a handful of Tiger tanks of the 101st SS Heavy Panzer Battalion, one of them commanded by Michael Wittmann. Fighting through the village afterwards cost the Germans several tanks in turn, but the British brigade was left exposed on a ridge without infantry support and was withdrawn the next day under heavy attack.

Around thirty British tanks and as many other vehicles were lost. The 7th Armoured Division's commander and corps commander were both replaced within weeks.

The action is remembered less for its scale than for what it showed about armour in the bocage, where hedged banks and sunken lanes gave a concealed defender the first shot at close range, and where a division that had fought in the open desert had to learn a different war.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Villers-Bocage).

name: Fall of Cherbourg
summary: The Cotentin port surrendered on 27 June 1944 with its harbour so thoroughly demolished that it took until autumn to work at capacity.
body:
Part of the [D-Day landings](event:d-day). Cherbourg, at the tip of the Cotentin peninsula, was the deep-water port the Normandy campaign had been planned around: the artificial Mulberry harbours were a stopgap, and one of the two had been wrecked by a gale on 19 June.

The American VII Corps cut the peninsula on 18 June 1944, isolating the port, and turned north. Hitler ordered the garrison to hold to the last and to destroy the harbour if it could not. It took a week to fight through the ring of outer forts; the commander, Karl-Wilhelm von Schlieben, surrendered on 26 June and the last resistance in the arsenal ended on the 29th. Some 39,000 prisoners were taken.

The engineers had done their work first. Cranes were toppled, quays cratered, the basins filled with sunken ships and the approaches mined, in what Allied engineers described as the most thorough demolition they encountered. Salvage and repair took months, and Cherbourg did not handle cargo in quantity until the autumn, by which time the armies were already east of the Seine and their supply problem had moved with them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cherbourg).
